title: PART I

nodes.title: Boeing Business and Operating Segments
nodes.summary: Boeing is a major aerospace company organized into three segments. Commercial Airplanes develops and sells passenger and cargo jets, including the 737, 767, 777 and 787, while developing the 777X and 737-7/-10. Defense, Space & Security develops and modifies military aircraft, weapons, defense and intelligence systems, cyber solutions, satellites and space exploration products. Global Services supports commercial and defense customers through logistics, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, parts, training, documentation and digital analytics.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The company owns numerous patents, licenses others’ patents, and both licenses intellectual property to and from third parties. The U.S. government may use or authorize use of inventions developed under government contracts. Unpatented research, development and engineering expertise, trademarks, trade secrets, and other rights also support the business. Although intellectual property is important across its businesses, the company does not believe the expiration or termination of any single right or patent license would materially affect operations.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.summary: Boeing had about 172,000 employees at year-end 2024, with workforce demographics, roughly 58,000 union members, and major IAM, SPEEA and UAW agreements and expiration dates described. A 2024 IAM District 751 strike ended with contract ratification after disrupting production and prompting hiring freezes and planned workforce reductions. Boeing outlines its compensation, benefits, recognition, learning and development programs, including 5.9 million training hours and 14,000 tuition-assistance users. It also emphasizes workplace safety, quality, integrity, sustainability, annual Code of Conduct commitments, and channels for employees to raise concerns.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The commercial aircraft market is highly competitive, with Airbus and Chinese entrants challenging the company, which aims to compete through better products, processes, cost reductions, and customer value. Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS) faces major U.S. and international rivals, including occasional competitor partnerships, and expects competition to remain strong through 2025. Boeing Global Services (BGS) serves competitive commercial and defense markets with lifecycle services, from training and logistics to maintenance, upgrades, and daily operations, and plans to grow share through customer satisfaction and productivity.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: The company operates under extensive U.S. and international regulation. Government contracts may be terminated for convenience or default, with different payment, reprocurement-cost and damages consequences. Commercial aircraft must meet aviation production, quality, airworthiness and safety rules; after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident, the FAA investigated Spirit and increased oversight, limiting Boeing rate increases and new lines pending compliance. Environmental laws may raise costs and require investment; compliance and remediation are recurring, and stricter standards or newly found contamination could materially affect results. Non-U.S. sales face trade, investment, anti-corruption and other regulations, plus currency, political and economic risks.

nodes.title: Raw Materials, Parts and Subassemblies
nodes.summary: The company depends on suppliers and subcontractors for the availability and quality of essential materials, parts, and subassemblies. Key aerospace raw materials include aluminum and titanium in sheet, plate, forging, and extrusion forms, plus carbon- and boron-based composites. Alternative sources generally exist, but qualifying them may take a year or more. Many major components and equipment items are sole-sourced, so the company works with a limited number of sole-source suppliers to maintain supply continuity.

nodes.title: Suppliers
nodes.summary: Boeing relies on domestic and international suppliers and subcontractors to meet cost, quality, performance, and delivery requirements; despite oversight systems, failures and rising prices can harm products, schedules, profitability, and customer commitments. Affordable energy is also necessary. Its business is not materially seasonal. The text directs readers to Part III for executive-officer information and provides Boeing’s incorporation history, headquarters, contact details, website and SEC filing access, noting website content is not incorporated into the report. It explains how to identify forward-looking statements, their assumptions and uncertainties, risks that may cause actual results to differ, and that Boeing generally has no duty to update them.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
nodes.summary: The section introduces investment risks and uncertainties that could materially affect the company’s business, financial position, operating results, and cash flows. It advises reviewing these risks alongside the report’s other disclosures, including management’s discussion and analysis and the consolidated financial statements and notes. Because known and unknown risks may affect outcomes, past financial results and historical trends may not predict future performance or trends.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Operations
We depend heavily on commercial airlines, subjecting us to unique risks.
key_items: Market conditions have a significant impact on demand for our commercial aircraft and related services

We enter into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which subjects us to losses if we have cost overruns or if increases in our costs exceed the applicable escalation rate
We derive a significant portion of our revenues from a limited number of commercial airlines
nodes.summary: The company’s dependence on commercial airlines exposes it to cyclical market and customer risks. Aircraft demand depends on economic growth, political stability, airline traffic and profitability, financing, trade and geopolitical conditions, technology, competition, fuel and inflation costs, security and health crises, sustainability, regulation, and reputation. Downturns or customer distress may reduce, delay, or cancel orders and payments, lowering revenue, profits, cash flow, and backlog, with effects spanning years. Fixed-price contracts use indexed escalation that may not keep pace with actual cost increases, affecting revenue and margins. Revenue concentration, uncertain options and commitments, airline fleet decisions, consolidation, financial challenges, and rising fuel and other costs further threaten results.

nodes.title: Our Commercial Airplanes business depends on our ability to maintain a healthy production system, ensure every airplane in our production system conforms to exacting specifications,
key_items: We must minimize disruption caused by production changes, achieve operational stability and implement productivity improvements in order to meet customer demand and maintain our profitabillty
If our commercial aircraft fail to satisfy performance and reliability requirements and/or potentially required sustainability standards, we could face additional costs and/or lower revenues
nodes.summary: Boeing’s commercial airplane business depends on safe, reliable production, supplier coordination, skilled labor, regulatory compliance, and meeting cost, rate, and delivery targets. Quality failures—including FAA findings after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident—led to increased oversight and slower 737 production, harming and potentially continuing to harm financial results and cash flow. Delays in certifying new aircraft and derivatives could worsen financial performance and trigger customer compensation, order substitutions, or cancellations. Production-rate changes, supplier constraints, labor instability, inflation, and operational disruption can delay deliveries, raise costs, reduce productivity, and hurt revenue and margins. Failure to meet performance, reliability, or potential sustainability standards could also increase costs and reduce revenue.

nodes.title: Changes in levels of U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities, as well as significant delays in U.S. government appropriations, could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The company relies substantially on U.S. government revenue, especially DoD, NASA, and other agency contracts, so unpredictable defense spending, political and economic factors, spending caps, and delayed appropriations pose risks. Continuing resolutions or shutdowns may delay programs, payments, aircraft deliveries and certification, contract work, and future orders, with uncertain operational effects. Shifting acquisition priorities, budget cuts, and tradeoffs among modernization, sustainment, and emerging technologies could reduce, cancel, or delay programs and materially affect finances and cash flow. The DoD’s focus on affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and technical data and software requirements may challenge the company and suppliers, potentially reducing revenue and market share.

nodes.title: Supplier Dependencies and Labor Risks
key_items: Our ability to deliver products and services that satisfy customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of highly skilled labor, raw materials and other components.

Some of our and our suppliers’ workforces are represented by labor unions. Work stoppages by our employees have adversely affected and could continue to adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and/or cash flows. Future work stoppages by our or our suppliers’ employees could also adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The company depends on suppliers and subcontractors for materials, components, and services, and on skilled labor; financial problems, inflation, resource constraints, quality issues, disruptions, tariffs, or reliance on single sources could delay deliveries, raise costs, and harm results. Union representation and work stoppages can disrupt operations and supplier activity, limit workforce flexibility, delay products, and strain customer relationships. A 2024 IAM 751 strike halted much production, contributed to significant cash use, and the new contract and employee pay increases continue to pressure finances; further stoppages are possible.

nodes.title: Competition within our markets and with respect to our products and services may reduce our future contracts and sales.
nodes.summary: The company warns that intense competition may reduce future contracts, sales, revenue, and market share. Competitors may have stronger or more specialized capabilities. BCA faces aggressive international rivals; BDS expects competition to intensify due to industry consolidation, changing acquisition and budget priorities, and customer cost pressures; BGS competes with many of the same strong U.S. and international firms. Rising international competition, cross-border consolidation, and U.S. procurement and compliance requirements may also limit cost competitiveness abroad. Success against current and future competitors is uncertain.

nodes.title: We derive a significant portion of our revenues from non-U.S. sales and are subject to the risks of doing business in other countries.
nodes.summary: In 2024, non-U.S. customers, including foreign military sales, generated about 46% of revenue, and international sales are expected to remain significant. Risks include regulatory and government-policy changes, geopolitical and trade disputes, tariffs and other trade restrictions, local sourcing and industrial-participation requirements, currency fluctuations, political and budget volatility, reliance on foreign representatives, customer financing and funding uncertainty, taxes, legal compliance, and operational complexity, as well as terrorism, war, epidemics, and other conflicts. U.S.-China tariffs have affected some aircraft parts; Boeing uses duty-drawback procedures to mitigate costs. Continued trade tensions could disrupt Chinese aircraft deliveries or orders, reducing deliveries or market share and materially harming financial results and cash flows.

nodes.title: We use estimates and make assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs. Changes in our estimates and/or assumptions could adversely affect our future financial results.
nodes.summary: The text explains that contract and program accounting relies on uncertain estimates of revenues, costs, schedules, performance incentives, claims, award fees, production quantities, pricing, and costs; changes in assumptions or circumstances could materially harm future results. Commercial aircraft program accounting aggregates production, tooling, nonrecurring, and warranty costs, with estimates affected by production, market, supplier, certification, and other factors. It also describes risks in the pending Spirit AeroSystems acquisition, including completion conditions, regulatory delays, termination, debt, integration, and failure to achieve benefits, and broader risks that mergers, acquisitions, alliances, joint ventures, or divestitures may create liabilities, costs, or losses.

nodes.title: Acquisition and Strategic Transaction Risks
key_items: Our pending acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc. (Spirit) subjects us to various risks and uncertainties, including risks that we may not complete the acquisition or realize the anticipated benefits in the expected timeframe or at all.
We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures.
nodes.summary: The page references accounting disclosures, then outlines risks of Boeing’s pending all-stock Spirit acquisition: closing conditions and regulatory or termination hurdles may delay or prevent completion; failure could consume resources and harm stakeholder sentiment or stock price; completion entails debt, integration, operational, expense, and financial risks that could prevent expected synergies and quality improvements. It also describes risks that mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, alliances, or divestitures may not deliver benefits, including integration and performance problems, liabilities, cybersecurity issues, transaction costs, impairments, guarantees, partner or management issues, and ongoing obligations after divestitures.

The section describes risks from reliance on cyclical commercial-airline demand, customer concentration, uncertain orders and contract cost escalation; production quality, safety, certification, supplier coordination, labor, delivery and rate challenges; volatile U.S. government budgets and acquisition priorities; supplier, workforce and strike disruptions; intense competition; and international sales exposure to geopolitical, trade, regulatory, currency, funding and operational risks. It also explains uncertainty in contract and program accounting estimates and the risks of the pending Spirit AeroSystems acquisition and other strategic transactions, including delays, failure to close or realize benefits, integration problems, liabilities, costs and debt.

nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from reliance on U.S. government contracts (42% of 2024 revenue), including changing procurement rules and compliance costs, funding cuts or contract modification/termination, audits and investigations with potential repayments, penalties, suspension, or reputational damage. It also describes fixed-price contract cost-overrun risks, citing $5 billion in 2024 losses on five major BDS programs and ongoing production, supplier, labor, and technical challenges; cost-type contract risks to fees and profits; and satellite in-orbit incentive payments that may be forfeited or refunded if performance criteria are not met.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Technology, Security and Business Disruptions
key_items: Managing a complex, global IT infrastructure exposes us to a variety of risks that could negatively impact our business.
Compromised or unauthorized access of our, our customers’ and/or our suppliers’ systems or data could negatively impact our business.
Business disruptions could seriously affect our future sales and financial condition or increase our costs and expenses.
nodes.summary: Boeing’s decentralized global IT infrastructure creates risks of inefficiency, disruption, errors, fraud, unauthorized access, breaches, and regulatory or privacy noncompliance. Evolving cyber threats—including sophisticated actors, AI-enabled attacks, ransomware, phishing, and supply-chain or third-party incidents—could expose sensitive data or intellectual property, disrupt or compromise operations and services, and cause reputational, regulatory, or financial harm; existing safeguards may not prevent or timely address incidents. Past subsidiary incidents were not materially damaging, but future impacts could be. Disruptions from security threats, extreme weather and climate change, natural disasters, pandemics, or other crises could affect Boeing and suppliers, delay delivery, raise costs, reduce sales, and damage reputation.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
key_items: The outcome of litigation and of government inquiries and investigations involving our business is unpredictable, and an adverse decision in any such matter could have a material effect on our financial position and results of operations.
Our operations expose us to the risk of material environmental liabilities.
We may be adversely affected by global climate change or by legal, regulatory or market responses to such change.
nodes.summary: The text outlines legal, regulatory and environmental risks: litigation, government inquiries and investigations may divert resources or result in adverse rulings that materially affect finances, operations or cash flows. Environmental laws may expose the company to cleanup costs, penalties and third-party claims, including liabilities from past operations, acquisitions or indemnities; new rules or discoveries could increase costs. Climate change, ESG expectations, regulation, market and policy responses, emissions standards, carbon pricing, disclosure rules, chemical restrictions, and water and waste requirements may raise costs, harm reputation or competitiveness, and disrupt supply chains, production or data facilities. Failure to meet or report sustainability commitments may also damage reputation or access to capital.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity
We may be unable to effectively manage our liquidity, which could adversely affect our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The company warns that liquidity constraints could harm its business, financial position, and results. It relies on capital markets, expects continued negative operating cash flow while increasing aircraft production, and faces $53.9 billion in debt, $13.6 billion in principal payments due within three years, $17.1 billion in aircraft financing commitments, Spirit’s expected net debt, and potential annual preferred-stock dividends of up to $345 million through October 2027. Unpaid dividends accumulate and may trigger preferred holders’ rights to elect two directors. Additional funding needs could require refinancing, delayed investment, or securities issuance on unfavorable or dilutive terms; limited market access or higher borrowing costs could worsen liquidity. Credit-rating downgrades, weak performance, production delays, market disruption, and changing demand could raise borrowing costs and restrict financing. Investment-grade ratings are not assured, and further actual or anticipated downgrades could impair liquidity, financial position, and market access.

nodes.title: Pension, Insurance, and Financing Risks
key_items: Substantial pension and other postretirement benefit obligations have a material impact on our earnings, shareholders’ equity and cash flows from operations, and could have significant adverse impacts in future periods.
Our insurance coverage may be inadequate to cover all significant risk exposures.
A significant portion of our customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in certain types of Boeing aircraft, which exposes us to concentration risks.
nodes.summary: The page outlines risks from pension and postretirement obligations, whose costs and contributions depend on assumptions and market conditions and can affect earnings, equity, cash flows, and contract profitability. Insurance may not cover significant product-related liabilities, particularly outside U.S. SAFETY Act protections. Customer financing is concentrated by customer, region, aircraft type, and credit quality; defaults, lease nonrenewals, or difficulty redeploying aircraft could materially harm financial results.

nodes.title: Share Dilution and Preferred Stock Priority
key_items: The issuance of common stock upon the closing of the Spirit acquisition and upon conversion of our Mandatory convertible preferred stock, and the possibility of the sale or issuance of our common stock in the future, could cause dilution to the interests of our existing shareholders.
Our common stock ranks junior to the Mandatory convertible preferred stock with respect to dividends and amounts payable in the event of our liquidation, dissolution or winding-up of our affairs.
nodes.summary: The Spirit acquisition, conversion of mandatory convertible preferred stock, and equity awards may lead to significant future common stock issuance and dilute existing shareholders. Spirit shares will be exchanged at a price-based ratio, while preferred shares convert automatically around October 15, 2027, or may be converted earlier at a specified minimum rate, subject to adjustments. Common stock ranks behind preferred stock for dividends and liquidation distributions: common dividends are generally barred until preferred dividends are paid or reserved, and preferred holders receive $1,000 per share plus unpaid accumulated dividends before common holders receive assets.

The section describes liquidity risks from negative operating cash flow, substantial debt and financing commitments, preferred dividends, refinancing needs, market access, rising borrowing costs, and credit-rating downgrades. It covers pension and postretirement obligations, potentially insufficient insurance, and customer financing exposure to defaults, lease nonrenewals, and aircraft redeployment challenges. It also warns that the Spirit acquisition, preferred-stock conversion, and equity awards may dilute common shareholders, whose dividend and liquidation rights rank behind preferred holders.

Item 1C. Cybersecurity

nodes.title: Risk Management and Strategy
nodes.summary: The company’s cybersecurity strategy focuses on detecting and responding to threats, managing risk, and maintaining resilience. Its risk-based controls and safeguards draw on NIST and other standards, monitoring, training, oversight, audits, threat intelligence, partnerships, and third-party resources. The company continuously assesses threats to its systems, products, and operations, integrates cyber risks into board-overseen enterprise and compliance risk programs, uses consultants and incident-response exercises, and trains employees annually with monthly phishing simulations. A cross-functional program assesses risks from select suppliers and service providers and promotes recognized security standards. Past incidents have not materially affected the company, but future incidents could; prevention and response processes cannot guarantee otherwise.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.summary: The Board oversees risk, delegating cybersecurity oversight to the Audit and Aerospace Safety Committees, which report to the full Board. The Audit Committee reviews cyber risk processes, receives bimonthly management briefings, conducts focused strategy reviews, and is alerted to potentially material events. The Aerospace Safety Committee monitors threats to product safety; both committees update the Board, and the CIDO provides annual briefings. Management’s monthly Global Security Governance Council coordinates enterprise cyber policy, strategy, incident prevention and response, and reports progress to the Executive Council. Interim CSO Trent Cox chairs it and oversees an integrated security program; experienced senior leaders represent technology, engineering, safety, and product security. IT, security, audit, and legal teams coordinate timely issue handling and required regulatory reporting.

Major sites across the businesses totaled over 88 million square feet, spanning listed U.S. and international locations. Runways and taxiways are generally jointly used under long-term leases on others’ airport properties, and the U.S. government provides some facilities and equipment for contract work. Legal proceedings are addressed by reference to Note 22 of the consolidated financial statements; mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: The company is a global aerospace leader in commercial aircraft, defense, space, and services, operating mainly in the U.S. with international partners. Its strategy focuses on Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, and Global Services. After a January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door-plug accident, the FAA grounded affected aircraft, required inspections, and investigated quality controls; fleets returned to service after enhanced inspections. The company submitted a safety and quality plan, slowed production, and implemented workforce training and process and culture improvements, significantly affecting 2024 financial results and cash flows. A September–November IAM 751 strike paused production of commercial and derivative defense aircraft; production resumed in December, but reduced deliveries and contract and pay increases further adversely affected financial performance.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: Global air travel exceeded 2019 levels in 2024, led by domestic and single-aisle travel; international and wide-body markets are recovering, though China remains below pre-pandemic levels. Strong airline demand and improving profitability support the outlook, but high costs, economic and geopolitical uncertainty, and supply-chain, labor, quality, and inflation pressures are hurting productivity, results, and cash flows. Long-term commercial demand remains positive, with projected 3.2% fleet growth and demand for about 43,975 new airplanes over 20 years, subject to significant external risks. BDS sees stable global defense demand but faces production disruptions and charges on development and mature programs. BGS expects strong commercial revenues and stable government-services demand.

Boeing Financial Results and Revenues
nodes.summary: Presents 2022–2024 GAAP results (operating loss and margin, effective tax rate, shareholder net loss and diluted loss per share) and non-GAAP core operating loss, margin and loss per share, excluding certain pension and postretirement benefit costs, with references to reconciliations. Revenue rose in 2023 on growth across all segments. Recovery depends on delivery increases, supply-chain stabilization and reduced labor instability.

nodes.title: Loss From Operations
nodes.summary: The table reports 2022–2024 segment operating results, GAAP loss from operations, FAS/CAS pension and postretirement service-cost adjustments, and non-GAAP core operating loss; the adjustment reconciles GAAP service costs with costs allocated to segments, and core operating loss excludes it. In 2024, GAAP loss worsened by $9.934 billion versus 2023: BCA losses grew due to program charges, 737-9 customer considerations, fewer deliveries, production disruption, and higher R&D, partly offset by lower abnormal production costs; BDS losses grew due to unfavorable fixed-price contract adjustments; BGS earnings rose on commercial services; and unallocated losses increased. In 2023, GAAP loss improved by $2.746 billion versus 2022, led by improved BDS contract adjustments, BCA deliveries and costs, and BGS services, partly offset by higher unallocated deferred-compensation expense. Core operating loss worsened by $9.982 billion in 2024 and improved by $2.833 billion in 2023, mainly reflecting segment operating-loss changes.

nodes.title: Unallocated Items, Eliminations and Other
nodes.summary: The text reports unallocated items, eliminations and other expenses/income for 2022–2024 and explains year-over-year changes: share-based plan income rose in 2024 and expense fell in 2023 due to fewer awards/grants and allocation timing; deferred compensation expense changes reflected stock-price and market conditions; R&D expense rose with enterprise product spending; and other unallocated expense increased in 2024, mainly due to a $244 million potential DOJ-agreement fine, while largely unchanged in 2023. It also presents pension costs allocated to business segments, FAS/CAS service-cost adjustments, and net periodic pension benefit costs, noting their relative stability and the reasons for the 2023 adjustment decline. Further postretirement-plan discussion is in Note 17.

nodes.title: Other Earnings Items
nodes.summary: The table reports Boeing’s 2022–2024 operating losses, other income, interest and debt expense, pretax losses, income tax benefits or expenses, net losses, noncontrolling interests, and losses attributable to shareholders. It explains changes in non-operating pension income ($476 million in 2024, $529 million in 2023, and $881 million in 2022) and postretirement income ($73 million in 2024; $58 million in 2023 and 2022), citing effects from returns, interest costs, and amortization. Interest and debt expense rose in 2024 due to higher average debt and fell in 2023 due to lower balances. It directs readers to Notes 17 and 5 for postretirement plans and income taxes.

nodes.title: Total Costs and Expenses (“Cost of Sales”)
nodes.summary: Cost of sales includes materials, labor, overhead, and subcontracting; BCA uses program accounting for commercial aircraft, long-term contracts recognize costs as incurred, and spare parts use average cost. Cost of sales was $70.070 billion in 2024 (103.0% of revenue), down $1.562 billion from 2023, but its revenue share rose due to 777X and 767 reach-forward losses, lower BCA margins, and BDS development charges. In 2023, costs rose $6.992 billion from 2022 as BCA and BGS revenues increased, while the revenue share fell mainly due to lower BDS development charges. R&D rose from $2.852 billion in 2022 to $3.377 billion in 2023 and $3.812 billion in 2024, driven chiefly by 777X work and enterprise product-development investment.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: Cost of sales fell $1.562 billion in 2024 versus 2023, mainly due to lower BCA revenue, partly offset by reach-forward losses on the 777X and 767 programs and higher BDS fixed-price development charges. Cost of sales as a percentage of revenue rose due to those losses and charges and lower BCA margins. In 2023, cost of sales rose $6.992 billion from 2022 as BCA and BGS revenues increased, partly offset by lower BDS development charges; its revenue percentage fell mainly because BDS charges were lower. Research and development expense totaled $3.812 billion in 2024, $3.377 billion in 2023, and $2.852 billion in 2022, with segment-level amounts shown. Annual increases of $435 million and $525 million, respectively, were primarily driven by the 777X program and enterprise product-development investment.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: The table reports backlog at December 31, 2024 and 2023 by business segment and type. Total backlog rose to $521.3 billion from $520.2 billion; contractual backlog increased to $498.8 billion, while unobligated backlog was largely unchanged at $22.5 billion. Contractual backlog excludes options, unexecuted announced orders, terminable orders, and unauthorized government funding. Its increase reflected higher BDS and BGS backlog, partly offset by lower BCA backlog. Backlog may decline or orders be canceled due to delivery or production delays and delayed entry into service of the 777X, 737-7, or 737-10.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from uncertain U.S. funding decisions: a shutdown after March 14, 2025, Treasury debt-limit disruption, or FRA spending caps and potential sequestration could delay payments, disrupt operations and contracts, and materially affect financial results. It describes rising global trade risks, including tariffs, restrictions, sanctions, and stalled U.S.–China relations, and the need to monitor and mitigate effects. Inflation, supply disruptions, labor instability, and supplier financial distress have reduced productivity and contributed to program losses, including a $1.77 billion T-7A reach-forward loss. For Commercial Airplanes, intense competition and pricing pressure persist; about 80% of backlog is with non-U.S. airlines, making global market access critical.

nodes.title: BCA Operating Results, Revenues, and Deliveries
nodes.summary: The page reports BCA results for 2022–2024: revenues, share of company revenue, operating losses and margins, and R&D. Revenue fell in 2024 due to lower deliveries and 737-9 grounding-related considerations, after rising in 2023 on higher 787 deliveries. It lists annual and cumulative deliveries by aircraft program. The 2024 operating loss reflected 777X/767 reach-forward losses, grounding considerations, lower deliveries and margins, production disruption, and higher R&D, partly offset by lower abnormal production costs. The 2023 loss improved versus 2022 through higher deliveries and lower expenses, partly offset by R&D; abnormal production costs by program are detailed for both years.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: Defines backlog as probable-to-collect transaction prices for unsatisfied or partly satisfied obligations with contingencies cleared; excludes contingent prospective orders, options, customer-financing orders, and terminable orders. Notes customer delivery remedies and backlog adjustments under ASC 606. BCA backlog fell from $440.5 billion in 2023 to $435.2 billion in 2024, reflecting ASC 606 exclusions, cancellations and price decreases, partly offset by new orders exceeding deliveries; cancellations were $11.3 billion and net ASC 606 adjustments $16.6 billion, mainly involving 737 and 777X aircraft. Delivery, production and entry-into-service delays may reduce backlog or cause cancellations. Explains program accounting quantities, their role in revenue, cost and gross-margin estimates, the demand factors considered, quarterly review, and inclusion of delivered, contracted and anticipated units. A 2022–2024 table lists accounting quantities, undelivered firm orders and cumulative firm orders for 737, 747, 767, 777, 777X and 787; notes military-derivative and customer-financing order treatment, 737 model order percentages, and 747 production and final-delivery dates.

nodes.title: Program Highlights
nodes.summary: The text reviews Boeing’s commercial programs and fleet support. After the January 2024 737-9 door-plug accident, the FAA grounded affected aircraft, investigated quality systems, increased oversight, and restricted production increases; Boeing submitted a safety and quality plan, slowed production, and began improvement measures. IAM 751’s strike paused production until December. The company expects to deliver older 737-8 inventory in 2025; delayed 737-7/-10 certification and their engine anti-ice solution remain subject to FAA timing. These issues adversely affected finances. For the 767, production resumed in December, and Boeing now expects to end freighter production in late 2026 or early 2027, recording reach-forward losses. The 777 accounting quantity rose; 777/777X production resumed, but flight tests and certifications were delayed, deliveries pushed back, and production slowed, causing substantial losses and risk of further losses. The 787 accounting quantity rose, but supply constraints and seat delays reduced production and deliveries; rework of older inventory is planned, with related costs expensed. Fleet support includes training, field, engineering, information, and technical services throughout aircraft life; costs are expensed as incurred and historically represent about 1% of consolidated product and service costs.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: FY2024 appropriations enacted in March 2024 provided $844 billion for DoD and $25 billion for NASA, including funding for several Boeing programs. The FY2025 budget request sought $850 billion for DoD and $25 billion for NASA. Uncertainty over FY2025 and future agency funding could lead to cuts, cancellations, or delays, materially affecting Boeing’s results, finances, or cash flows. International defense demand is supported by security challenges and modernization needs; BDS sees opportunities across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, with non-U.S. customers representing 29% of its year-end 2024 backlog.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The text reports results for 2022–2024: revenue of $23.162B, $24.933B, and $23.918B (35%, 32%, and 36% of company revenue), operating losses of $3.544B, $1.764B, and $5.413B, and margins of (15.3)%, (7.1)%, and (22.6)%, respectively. It cautions that long-term contracts and varying schedules and funding structures make period results and backlog comparisons unreliable indicators of future performance. It also lists annual deliveries by aircraft, satellite, and other production or remanufactured unit type, totaling 165 in 2022, 162 in 2023, and 112 in 2024.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BDS revenue fell $1.015 billion in 2024 versus 2023, mainly due to $909 million in higher unfavorable cumulative contract catch-up adjustments on five major fixed-price development programs; overall, such adjustments were $995 million worse. Revenue rose $1.771 billion in 2023 versus 2022, including a $1.767 billion increase from those programs, reflecting lower unfavorable adjustments and higher completion costs. Adjustments improved by $648 million in 2023, largely from lower development-program charges, partly offset by unfavorable performance elsewhere.

nodes.title: Loss From Operations
nodes.summary: BDS operating losses rose to $5.413 billion in 2024 from $1.764 billion in 2023, mainly due to larger unfavorable catch-up adjustments and $5.013 billion of losses across five fixed-price programs. In 2023, losses fell from $3.544 billion in 2022 as fixed-price charges declined, partly offset by weaker earnings elsewhere, higher expenses, and a $315 million satellite agreement impact. The text also reports equity-method income and $64.023 billion of year-end backlog. It outlines cost, schedule, technical, and future-loss risks in cost-type and fixed-price development programs. Global Services markets and trends include expected strong commercial revenue, fleet growth, aftermarket demand, analytics, predictive maintenance, and outsourced spare-parts management.

nodes.title: BDS Backlog and Program Risks
nodes.summary: The text notes improved cumulative contract catch-up adjustments and BDS equity-method investment income, then reports year-end backlog of $64.0 billion, up $5.0 billion year over year due to award timing, partly offset by recognized revenue. It outlines risks in complex development programs: cost-type contracts may face reduced fees, lower profits, or cancellation; fixed-price programs may incur reach-forward losses. Technical, quality, schedule, and cost issues could require additional losses, delay deliveries, trigger termination provisions, or otherwise materially harm financial results.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: BGS serves commercial and government aerospace markets through parts, logistics, maintenance, upgrades, training, and digital services. Commercial demand is expected to stay strong as aviation shifts to growth; fleet expansion, efficiency, predictive maintenance, and outsourced spares management support long-term demand. Government demand was stable in 2024; U.S. growth is expected to be flat, non-U.S. fleets to grow faster, and military retirements to drive aging-aircraft and capability-upgrade services. U.S. government spending uncertainty may delay programs. Competition is intense, pressuring prices, while global market access remains important. Revenues, operating earnings, and margins rose in 2024 and 2023, mainly on commercial services growth; contract catch-up adjustments were unfavorable. Backlog rose 8% to $21.4 billion at year-end 2024, mainly due to award timing.

nodes.title: BGS Market Outlook and Operating Results
nodes.summary: Government services demand was stable in 2024; U.S. growth is expected to be flat, while non-U.S. fleets grow faster, and aircraft retirements should boost maintenance and upgrade demand. U.S. government spending limits may delay programs. Aviation services competition pressures pricing, making global market access important. BGS revenue rose to $19.954 billion in 2024 from $19.127 billion in 2023 and $17.611 billion in 2022; operating earnings rose to $3.618 billion from $3.329 billion and $2.727 billion, with margins of 18.1%, 17.4%, and 15.5%. Increases were primarily driven by commercial services; unfavorable contract catch-up adjustments also affected year-over-year comparisons.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: BGS backlog rose 8% to $21.4 billion at year-end 2024, mainly due to award timing. The cash-flow summary shows operating cash used of $12.1 billion in 2024, versus cash provided of $6.0 billion in 2023 and $3.5 billion in 2022. The 2024 deterioration reflected commercial-aircraft production and delivery disruptions, a larger net loss, reach-forward losses, and unfavorable working-capital changes, especially inventory and payables; advances and progress billings partly offset these effects. Prior-year comparisons discuss revenue, inventory, accrued liabilities, customer concessions, and tax refunds. Supply-chain financing changes were not material. Investing cash use increased in 2024, mainly from investment contributions; capital spending rose and is expected to grow in 2025. Financing cash provided in 2024 chiefly came from equity and preferred-stock issuances and senior notes; debt balances increased, with less classified short-term. The text also reports employee tax-withholding share transfers and confirms no common dividends in 2022–2024.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The text outlines Boeing’s contractual obligations, liquidity, financing risks, pension funding, purchase commitments, industrial participation agreements, and off-balance-sheet guarantees. It reports 2024 operating cash use of $12.1 billion, driven by commercial-aircraft production and delivery disruptions, and a planned all-stock Spirit acquisition. Year-end liquidity included cash, short-term investments, and revolving-credit capacity; it details credit facilities, ratings, covenant compliance, borrowing risks, and available capacity. Pension plans were GAAP-underfunded but over 90% ERISA-funded, with no significant 2025 contributions expected. Purchase obligations cover recorded and unrecorded procurement and other commitments; industrial participation agreements totaled $15.5 billion, with no penalties incurred in 2024.

nodes.title: Commercial Commitments and Contingent Obligations
nodes.summary: Summarizes commercial commitments outstanding at December 31, 2024, including standby letters of credit, surety bonds, and aircraft financing commitments by expected funding period. Customer financing commitments were $17.1 billion, versus $17.0 billion in 2023; the company expects alternative financing and historically has funded few commitments, but cannot assure future funding will remain limited. Contingent obligations include pending legal proceedings, claims, and investigations, plus environmental remediation liabilities of $834 million. Related disclosures are referenced in the financial statement notes.

nodes.title: Core Operating Earnings/(Loss), Core Operating Margins and Core Earnings/(Loss) Per Share
nodes.summary: The text explains Boeing’s non-GAAP core operating earnings, margins and earnings per share, their exclusions, and the caution to assess them alongside GAAP results because definitions may differ across companies. Core operating measures exclude the FAS/CAS service-cost adjustment; core EPS also excludes non-operating pension and postretirement income. It describes how GAAP and CAS pension costs are calculated and allocated, and postretirement costs allocated. It reports 2022–2024 adjustment benefits and non-operating pension income, explaining year-over-year changes and directing readers to further disclosures. Management uses the measures to evaluate and forecast underlying performance, viewing unallocated benefit costs as primarily market-driven and not allocable to U.S. government contracts.

nodes.title: Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures to GAAP Measures
nodes.summary: Reconciles 2022–2024 non-GAAP core operating loss, margins, and loss per share to GAAP results, with adjustments for pension and postretirement service costs, non-operating benefit income, deferred taxes, and diluted shares. Notes that long-term contract accounting relies on estimates of revenue, costs, profit, and risks, reviewed quarterly; estimate changes can create catch-up adjustments or immediate losses. Reports large 2024, 2023, and 2022 operating-loss impacts, mainly from fixed-price development programs, and warns future losses are possible. A 1% change in profitable-contract gross margins would shift 2024 pretax income by about $290 million. Introduces program accounting’s requirement for reliable estimates across a defined program quantity.

nodes.title: Accounting for Long-term Contracts
nodes.summary: The text outlines critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and program accounting. Most BDS and some BGS contracts are single performance obligations recognized using estimated total revenue, costs, and profit. Estimates depend on contract terms, government cost rules, operational and economic factors, and are reviewed quarterly; revisions create cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate losses. Losses increased operating loss by $6.562 billion in 2024, $2.943 billion in 2023, and $5.253 billion in 2022, mainly on named fixed-price development programs, with future losses possible. Estimates are highly judgmental; a 1% margin change on profitable contracts would alter 2024 pretax income by about $290 million. Program accounting requires reliable estimates for a defined program quantity.

nodes.title: Program Accounting
nodes.summary: The text explains critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and program accounting. Long-term contract revenue, cost and profit estimates depend on contract terms, government rules, operational and economic assumptions, and are reviewed quarterly; estimate changes can trigger cumulative adjustments or immediate losses. It reports 2022–2024 contract adjustments and losses on named fixed-price development programs, warns of future risk, and quantifies the effect of a 1% margin change. Program accounting estimates production quantities, prices and costs using demand, supplier, production, regulatory and other factors; it discusses FAA limits on 737 production increases, certification delays for new aircraft, quarterly reassessment, loss recognition, 2024 charges on the 777X and 767, margin pressures, future risks, and the earnings impact of a 1% margin change.

nodes.title: Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Most employees formerly in defined benefit pension plans have moved to a company-funded defined contribution plan. Annual accounting measurements of pension obligations and assets rely on assumptions, and changes or actual-versus-expected differences can affect expense, obligations, and shareholders’ equity. A 25-basis-point discount-rate increase or decrease would reduce or raise the projected benefit obligation by $1.12 billion or $1.24 billion, respectively, with no significant pension-cost effect. A 25-basis-point change in expected asset returns would change 2024 pension cost by $143 million in the opposite direction. Note 17 provides the assumptions used over the past three years.

nodes.title: Deferred Income Taxes – Valuation Allowance
nodes.summary: At year-end 2024, the Company had $17.991 billion in deferred tax assets, $10.091 billion in liabilities, and a $7.837 billion valuation allowance. Quarterly recoverability assessments weigh positive and negative evidence; recent losses preclude projected earnings, and management estimates reversal timing using judgment-based methods. The allowance rose $3.287 billion, mainly for unrealizable credits and carryforwards; further increases may hurt earnings or comprehensive income. The text also discusses market risks: fixed-rate debt exposure is not material; foreign-currency and commodity hedges largely offset underlying risks (10% rate changes imply $428 million sensitivity for currency contracts and $28 million for commodity derivatives); deferred compensation liabilities of $1.7 billion have $168 million sensitivity to a 10% fund-value change, recorded in operating earnings.

nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page notes a $3.287 billion increase in the tax valuation allowance, mainly for 2024 tax credits and carryforwards that cannot yet be used; further allowances may reduce earnings or other comprehensive income until profitability is sustained. It then describes market risks: fixed-rate debt has no material interest-rate exposure; foreign-currency forwards hedge committed and forecasted receipts and payments, with a 10% exchange-rate change affecting unrealized losses by $428 million, offset by underlying transactions; commodity swaps and purchase contracts hedge production inputs, with a 10% price change affecting unrealized losses by $28 million, likewise offset. Together, both hedging arrangements create no material market risk.

nodes.title: Market Risk
nodes.summary: Deferred compensation plan participants may allocate funds among investments whose fair values fluctuate. At December 31, 2024, the marked-to-market liability was $1.7 billion; a 10% investment-value change would alter it by $168 million, with liability changes recorded in operating earnings. The text then provides the financial statements and supplementary data index, listing consolidated statements, segment data, Notes 1–23 on accounting policies and financial topics, and the independent auditors’ reports, with page references.

nodes.summary: The text reports Boeing’s 2024, 2023, and 2022 segment revenues and operating results, including segment and total losses, other income and expenses, taxes, net losses, noncontrolling interests, and preferred-stock dividends; it directs readers to Note 23 for further segment results. Note 1 describes consolidation and financial-statement presentation, three reportable segments, a cash-flow reclassification, estimates under U.S. GAAP, and use of contract duration as the operating cycle. It explains commercial-aircraft revenue allocation and recognition at customer acceptance, program accounting for costs, and customary customer deposits and progress payments; it begins describing BDS and BGS long-term contracts and their products and services.

nodes.title: Boeing Accounting Policies and Operating Cycle
nodes.summary: Boeing’s consolidated financial statements cover majority-owned subsidiaries and required variable interest entities, eliminate significant intercompany transactions, and report three segments. Supplier-notes-receivable cash investments were added as a cash-flow line, with prior periods reclassified. GAAP statements rely on estimates and assumptions affecting reported amounts and disclosures; actual results may differ. Certain current assets and liabilities are classified using contract or program duration as the operating cycle, generally longer than one year.

nodes.title: Revenue and Related Cost Recognition
nodes.summary: The text explains revenue and cost recognition for commercial aircraft, long-term contracts, commercial spare parts, customer services, concessions, contract assets/liabilities, leases and loans, and reinsurance. It covers transaction-price allocation, timing and methods of revenue recognition, payment terms, variable consideration, contract estimates, cumulative catch-up adjustments and loss provisions, including reported 2022–2024 impacts and significant program losses. It also describes receivable collectability, residual values, impairment, and research-and-development expense and customer-funded arrangements.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting for financing receivables, including net presentation, interest recognition, past-due and uncollectible criteria, non-accrual treatment, and residual-value estimates and impairments. It describes operating-lease revenue, asset depreciation, held-for-sale measurement, and impairment reviews. It also summarizes Astro Ltd.’s workers’ compensation reinsurance pool, reporting 2022–2024 revenues and costs net in operating costs, and research and development expense policies, customer-funded arrangements, and bid-and-proposal costs for those years.

nodes.title: Compensation, Tax, and Benefit Plan Policies
nodes.summary: Describes share-based compensation measurement and expense recognition for share- and cash-settled awards. Covers income tax provisions, uncertain tax positions, related interest and penalties, and deferred tax asset valuation allowances. Summarizes pension and other postretirement benefits, plan transitions, benefit calculations, actuarial assumptions and gains or losses, and balance-sheet presentation. Postemployment benefits such as severance or job training are accrued when payment is probable and estimable.

nodes.title: Environmental Remediation and Cash Accounting
nodes.summary: The page describes environmental obligations and remediation accounting: the company assesses liabilities and potential recoveries from responsible parties or insurers, accrues probable and estimable costs at its best estimate or the low end of a reasonable range, does not discount costs, and records recoveries when probable. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less. Eligible bank balances are aggregated, and negative balances, mainly uncleared checks, are reclassified to Accounts payable; these were $110 and $117 at year-end 2024 and 2023, respectively.

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.summary: Inventory accounting covers eligible engineering, production, tooling, overhead and reengineering costs, with abnormal or unrecoverable costs expensed; long-cycle costs may extend beyond one year. Commercial aircraft inventories include deferred early-production costs and supplier advances, with quarterly recoverability reviews and loss provisions for contracts or programs expected to lose money. Used aircraft, general materials and spare parts are valued at cost or lower of cost and net realizable value, with impaired stock written off; airline early issue sales consideration reduces revenue at delivery or is written off if unrecoverable. Probable-to-be-recovered precontract costs are capitalized, except start-up costs, and written off if recovery becomes unlikely. Property and equipment accounting describes cost, useful lives, depreciation and software amortization, plus held-for-sale valuation and impairment testing. Lease classification is assessed at inception; operating and finance lease assets and liabilities are reported in specified balance-sheet categories.

nodes.title: Inventory, Precontract Costs, and Fixed Assets
nodes.summary: The page describes inventory valuation and quarterly reviews for obsolete or impaired parts, treatment of impairment charges, and recognition and potential recovery or write-off of airline early issue sales consideration. Precontract costs are capitalized when future recovery is probable, except start-up costs, and written off if recovery becomes unlikely. Property and equipment accounting covers cost, depreciation lives and methods, software amortization, useful-life reviews, held-for-sale measurement, and impairment testing for assets held for use.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.summary: The text explains how leases are identified at inception and presented: operating lease assets and liabilities appear in other assets and accrued or long-term liabilities, while finance leases—primarily computer equipment—are recorded in property, plant and equipment and current or long-term debt. Operating lease assets and liabilities are recognized at commencement using the estimated present value of payments and the incremental borrowing rate; variable costs are expensed as incurred. Lease terms include extension or termination options when exercise is reasonably certain, and operating lease expense is straight-lined. Real-property lease and non-lease components are treated as a single lease component.

nodes.title: Asset Retirement Obligations
nodes.summary: The company records known asset retirement obligations whose fair value can be reasonably estimated, including asbestos removal, decommissioning, and lease restoration; recorded amounts are immaterial. Known conditional obligations lacking sufficient information on settlement timing or method are not recorded until estimable. Potential undiscovered obligations, such as unknown asbestos, are also excluded from the financial statements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for goodwill and acquired intangibles: indefinite-lived assets are tested annually and upon triggering events, with goodwill testing using qualitative or quantitative methods; the 2024 test found reporting-unit fair values substantially above carrying values, though Military Aircraft had $1,295 goodwill and negative carrying value. It describes IPR&D impairment, reclassification and amortization, finite-lived intangible useful lives and impairment tests. Investment policies cover time deposits, available-for-sale debt, equity-method and other equity investments, impairment, and operating versus non-operating income classification. Derivatives are measured at fair value; cash-flow hedge gains or losses are deferred and later recognized in earnings, while non-designated aluminum and other derivatives’ fair-value changes enter earnings immediately.

nodes.title: Investment and Derivative Accounting
nodes.summary: Finite-lived acquired intangible assets are amortized over specified useful lives and tested for impairment when indicators arise, with losses measured against fair value if carrying amounts are unrecoverable. Investments accounting covers held-to-maturity time deposits; fair-value available-for-sale debt securities, including impairment and gain/loss treatment; equity-method and other equity investments; and operating versus non-operating income classification. Derivatives are recognized at fair value: cash-flow hedge gains and losses are initially reported in comprehensive income and later earnings, while non-designated aluminum agreements and other derivatives have fair-value changes recorded immediately in earnings.

nodes.title: Financial Asset Allowances and Aircraft Trade-ins

nodes.summary: The page explains quarterly assessment of credit-loss allowances using customer creditworthiness, receivable characteristics, loss estimates, and collateral values, including aircraft-specific judgments and agreements allowing other customer or supplier assets to cover collateral shortfalls. It also describes trade-in commitments for used aircraft, revenue adjustments and possible cost-of-products charges, accrued liability estimates, and valuation methods based on aircraft attributes, market conditions, resale, leasing, or scrap prospects, updated quarterly.

nodes.title: Warranties, Supplier Penalties, and Guarantees
nodes.summary: Describes warranty coverage for commercial and military products, warranty periods, estimates and liabilities, exceptional fleet-wide issues, and aircraft performance guarantees treated as warranties. It explains how customer payments reduce revenue, supplier claims reduce product costs and are included in program estimates. Supplier penalties are accrued when probable and reasonably estimable. Guarantees are initially recorded at fair value; credit-guarantee losses reflect default risk and expected recovery, with contingent-loss liabilities reassessed quarterly.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Spirit Acquisition
nodes.summary: Boeing agreed on June 30, 2024, to acquire Spirit in an all-stock deal valued at about $4.7 billion ($37.25 per share), assuming Spirit’s net debt. The exchange ratio ranges from 0.18 to 0.25 Boeing shares based on a 15-day average price, with specified price limits. The deal covers most Boeing-related commercial operations; Spirit separately plans to transfer Airbus work packages to Airbus, subject to definitive agreements and approvals, and sell other operations. Closing is expected mid-2025, subject to conditions; Spirit shareholders approved the deal January 31, 2025. Either party may terminate for specified uncured breaches or failure to close by the outside date, initially March 31, 2025, with up to three automatic extensions; certain regulatory failures can trigger a $300 million fee payable to Spirit. Boeing agreed to provide Spirit up to $1.067 billion in support, with $166 million undrawn, and disclosed related asset balances and recoverable advances. On January 22, 2025, repayment of $515 million was rescheduled to 2026, including $425 million originally due in 2024; outstanding balances become due April 1, 2026, if the merger terminates.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: The note details goodwill movements for 2023 and 2024 by business segment, including acquisitions, dispositions, and adjustments, with total goodwill of $8,084 at December 31, 2024. Indefinite-lived intangibles include trade names ($197) and in-process research and development for a next-generation air vehicle ($202), unchanged from 2023. It reports 2024 and 2023 gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization for acquired finite-lived intangibles, total amortization expense of $223 and $235, respectively, and estimated annual amortization of $207, $202, $182, $155, and $155 for 2025–2029.

nodes.title: Note 4 – Earnings Per Share

It presents 2022–2024 net losses, preferred dividends, participating-security earnings, weighted-average share counts, and basic and diluted loss per share. It also lists potential shares excluded as antidilutive due to strike prices, unmet performance conditions, or net losses, and notes participating securities include certain deferred-compensation-plan instruments.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Income Taxes
nodes.summary: Note 5 details income taxes for 2022–2024: U.S. and non-U.S. pretax losses, current and deferred tax benefits/expenses, cash tax payments/refunds, and reconciliation of statutory to actual tax, including the 2024 federal audit settlement. It lists deferred tax assets and liabilities, carryforward amounts and expirations, and valuation allowances, which increased amid cumulative losses and may rise further absent sustained profitability. It also covers non-U.S. reinvestment status, immaterial interest and penalties, unrecognized tax benefits, audit timelines, and the limited expected impact of global Pillar Two minimum-tax rules.

nodes.title: Note 6 – Accounts Receivable, net

Note 8 gives 2024 and 2023 inventory balances by category and identifies capitalized precontract costs related to Commercial Crew, T-7A, and KC-46A. nodes.title: Commercial Aircraft Programs

nodes.title: Note 9 – Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: Unbilled receivables rose from $8,317 in 2023 to $8,363 in 2024, mainly due to BDS revenue exceeding billings, partly offset by increased BGS billings. The table reports unbilled contract assets and claims, including current and after-one-year amounts and valuation allowances. Long-term commercial-incentive receivables were $63 and $42, respectively; claims are earned amounts subject to uncertainty in determination or realization. Advances and progress billings rose from $56,328 to $60,333, driven by BDS progress billings and BCA order advances. Revenue recognized from opening balances was $14,516 in 2024 and $15,298 in 2023.

nodes.title: Note 10 – Financing Receivables and Operating Lease Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 10 reports financing receivables and operating-lease equipment at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including balances, allowances, net amounts, and accumulated depreciation. It describes financing terms, extension/termination and purchase options, non-accrual and past-due balances, allowance changes, sales-type lease payment components, and interest income. It also presents 2024 receivables by credit rating and origination year, related default rates, portfolio concentration by aircraft model, impairment charges, lease income and commencement profits for 2022–2024, projected five-year-and-later cash flows by receivable type, and unguaranteed residual values.

nodes.title: Note 11 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 11 reports property, plant and equipment at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including land, buildings and improvements, machinery and equipment, construction in progress, gross assets, accumulated depreciation, and total net property, plant and equipment. Depreciation expense was $1,349 million in 2024, $1,328 million in 2023, and $1,396 million in 2022. Non-cash acquisitions were $76 million in 2024 and $124 million in 2023; related accounts payable was $591 million and $498 million, respectively.

nodes.title: Investments and Equity Method Holdings
nodes.summary: Reports investment balances at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including time deposits, equity method and available-for-sale debt investments, other investments, and restricted cash. Notes equity-method dividends and undistributed earnings, restricted funds’ purpose, and time-deposit purchases and maturities for 2022–2024. Describes quarterly credit-loss assessments, investment-grade status, no recognized allowance, and fair value approximating amortized cost. Lists equity-method holdings, ownership, segments, and balances, including United Launch Alliance.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 13 reports operating lease assets mainly for facilities, warehouses, and offices; lease expense, variable expense, cash payments, and noncash additions or modifications for 2022–2024; 2024 and 2023 right-of-use assets and current/noncurrent liabilities, lease terms and discount rates; balance-sheet classifications; future payment schedule and imputed interest; and $15 of office leases commencing in 2025. Note 14 lists 2024 and 2023 accrued liabilities by category, including forward-loss recognition, compensation, warranties, environmental costs, interest, customer concessions, retiree benefits, lease liabilities, and other amounts.

nodes.title: 737 MAX Customer Concessions and Other Considerations
nodes.summary: In 2024, Boeing recorded a $443 million earnings charge, net of insurance recoveries, for estimated customer considerations related to the Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident and grounding, reducing Sales of products. The liability declined from $1.864 billion to $1.327 billion in 2023 and from $1.327 billion to $641 million in 2024, reflecting payments, concessions and in-kind considerations, and estimate changes. At year-end 2024, $92 million remained under negotiation; $124 million is expected to be paid in cash, mainly in 2025, and the rest primarily through lower customer delivery payments.

nodes.title: Environmental
nodes.summary: Environmental remediation liabilities were $834 million at year-end 2024, reflecting payments and estimate changes; the high end of reasonably possible costs exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,002 million, versus $1,030 million in 2023. Estimates include remediation and up to 30 years of site operation and maintenance, but costs may rise, and some obligations cannot be estimated. Product warranty liabilities fell to $2,133 million in 2024 after additions, payments and estimate changes. Aircraft trade-in commitments let certain customers exchange used aircraft at specified prices; exercise likelihood is assessed using market information and reviewed quarterly. Commitments expire from 2025–2031; contractual totals were $1,393 million in 2024 and $1,415 million in 2023, with probable net payments of $275 million and $407 million, respectively, and related aircraft fair values of $270 million and $407 million.

nodes.title: Remediation, Warranty, and Aircraft Trade-In Liabilities
nodes.summary: Remediation liabilities reflect estimated site cleanup costs, including up to 30 years of operations and maintenance; actual costs may exceed estimates, and some obligations cannot be estimated. High-end possible costs exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,002 in 2024 and $1,030 in 2023. Warranty liabilities changed through deliveries, payments, and estimate revisions, ending at $2,133 in 2024 versus $2,448 in 2023. Aircraft trade-in commitments are assessed quarterly using quantitative and qualitative information; agreements expire from 2025–2031. Contractual commitments were $1,393 and $1,415, with probable net payments of $275 and $407 and related aircraft fair values of $270 and $407, respectively, in 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Financial Commitments and Insurance Obligations
key_items: Standby Letters of Credit and Surety Bonds
nodes.summary: Financing commitments for aircraft and refinancing totaled $17.124 billion in 2024 versus $17.003 billion in 2023, with estimated funding scheduled from 2025 onward; $13.798 billion involved customers below investment-grade credit, but no loss reserve was deemed necessary. Joint-venture capital contributions of $261 million are committed over eight years. Standby letters of credit and surety bonds totaled $2.991 billion in 2024 and $4.548 billion in 2023. Legacy COLI obligations remain, with policy cash values of $342 million and loans of $314 million in 2024 (2023: $360 million and $334 million); the net asset is reported in Other assets.

nodes.title: Supply Chain Financing Programs
nodes.summary: The Company’s supply chain financing program lets participating suppliers receive payment from an intermediary; the Company validates invoices and pays the intermediary based on invoice totals. Most amounts are due within 30–90 days, though payment terms can extend to 12 months. In 2024, the payable balance began at $2,871, increased by $12,476 in additions, decreased by $12,644 in payments, and ended at $2,703. The Company does not expect changes in program availability to significantly affect liquidity.

nodes.title: Government Assistance
nodes.summary: The company reports government incentives: South Carolina investment grants totaling $346, amortized through 2052, with related inventory, cost-of-sales benefits, and accrued-liability balances disclosed for 2024 and 2023. Missouri and Irving, Texas job-related tax refunds are available through 2031; cash receipts, cost-of-sales benefits, receivables, and $63 subject to employment-related clawback are reported. Queensland grants are available through 2032; 2023–2022 receipts benefited cost of sales, while a 2024 advance is a long-term liability subject to clawback. Missouri industrial revenue bonds financed St. Louis and St. Charles properties, providing sales-tax exemptions and property-tax abatements; the company holds the bonds and leases the properties, reports equal assets and liabilities net, and disclosed balances of $355 and $333 for 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Recoverable Costs on Government Contracts
nodes.summary: The text discusses government audits of incurred costs, potential disallowances, reserves, refunds or earnings charges, and impairment risk on roughly $500 in capital investments made ahead of contract awards. It explains fixed-price contract risks from uncertain costs, schedules, technical performance and negotiations. For the $4 billion VC-25B program, 2024 reach-forward losses rose $379 due to design changes and delays, with further losses possible. For the KC-46A, authorized contracts total about $29 billion; 2024 losses rose $2.002 billion, driven by factory and supply disruptions, supplier costs, labor stoppage and agreement impacts, production-rate allocations, and other cost increases.

nodes.title: Fixed-Price Contract Risks and VC-25B Losses
nodes.summary: The company had approximately $500 in capital investment at December 31, 2024, including expenditures at risk if anticipated contracts are not awarded. Fixed-price development contracts carry risks from uncertain costs, schedules, technical performance, and negotiations, potentially causing material charges, terminations, cancellations, or other exposure. The $4 billion VC-25B contract to modify two aircraft incurred additional reach-forward losses of $379 in 2024 and $482 in 2023; 2024 increases reflected engineering changes and delays, and further losses remain possible.

nodes.title: KC-46A Tanker
nodes.summary: The text reviews major defense and space programs, contract scope, losses and risks. KC-46A has 154 authorized aircraft; 2024 charges reflected factory disruption, supplier and labor costs, and lower production allocations, with further losses possible. MQ-25 includes seven EMD aircraft plus a 2024 cost-type modification; 2024 losses stemmed from production, design, and software challenges, with assembly and flight testing planned for 2025. T-7A’s five EMD aircraft are delivered, with testing ongoing; 2024 losses reflected supplier pricing, production, technical, and certification costs, plus precontract costs and supplier liabilities. The text begins a Commercial Crew update on Starliner.

nodes.title: MQ-25 and T-7A Program Contract Losses
key_items: T-7A Red Hawk EMD Contract & Production Options
nodes.summary: The MQ-25 Navy fixed-price EMD contract covers seven aircraft and test articles, with a later cost-type modification for two test aircraft and other work. Repeated reach-forward loss increases reflect production, design, software, and complexity challenges; initial units are expected to finish production and begin flight testing in 2025, alongside new-facility assembly. The T-7A EMD contract covers five aircraft and seven simulators; all five aircraft were delivered by year-end 2024, with testing ongoing. Loss increases in 2023–24 reflect production, technical, supplier-pricing, equipment, and certification costs. The company also reports capitalized precontract costs and supplier termination liabilities; further losses remain possible on both programs.

nodes.title: Commercial Crew
nodes.summary: NASA contracted the company to develop the CST-100 Starliner to carry crews to the ISS; its uncrewed orbital test was completed in 2022. A parachute issue delayed the crewed flight test and increased the 2023 reach-forward loss by $288. The flight launched and docked in June 2024, but after propulsion testing, Starliner returned uncrewed in September. Schedule delays, increased testing and certification costs, and higher post-certification mission costs raised the 2024 reach-forward loss by $523. At year-end, the company had $398 million in capitalized precontract costs and $150 million in potential supplier termination liabilities for unauthorized future missions, with further losses possible.

nodes.title: Severance
nodes.summary:
Severance
During the fourth quarter of 2024, we announced plans to reduce our overall workforce. As a result, we recorded $295 of severance benefits payable to employees expected to leave the Company through involuntary terminations by the first half of 2025. The severance packages are consistent with our ongoing compensation and benefits plans. The remaining liability at December 31, 2024, was $287.

nodes.title: Note 15 – Arrangements with Off-Balance Sheet Risk
nodes.summary: The company’s off-balance-sheet arrangements primarily comprise guarantees. At year-end 2024, third-party guarantee maximum potential payments were $295 million, versus $404 million in 2023; carrying liabilities were $14 million in both years, with estimated collateral/recourse proceeds also reported. Aircraft repurchase commitments, generally exercisable 10–15 years after delivery and conditional on a future aircraft-sale agreement, are typically below expected fair value and rarely become trade-ins. Credit guarantees cover lessee or debtor defaults and expire through 2036. Indefinite indemnities for pre-sale environmental and other matters cannot be quantified; estimable or probable claims are included in Note 14 environmental liabilities.

nodes.title: Note 16 – Debt
nodes.summary: Note 16 describes $10 billion of senior notes issued in 2024, their maturities, interest rates, ranking, and $9.9 billion net proceeds; revolving credit agreements opened, terminated, or retained, $10 billion of available credit, and covenant compliance. It reports interest incurred, paid, and capitalized for 2022–2024; short- and long-term debt balances, debt categories, and scheduled principal and lease payments. Note 17 summarizes defined-benefit pension participation, the transition of most participants to a company-funded defined-contribution plan, and trust funding and investment objectives for major pension plans.

nodes.title: Debt Balances and Scheduled Payments
nodes.summary: Presents debt balances at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including unsecured debt by interest-rate range and maturity, finance lease obligations, other notes, and total debt. Lists scheduled debt and other-note principal payments for 2025–2029, and finance lease payments through 2029 and thereafter, including total payments, imputed interest, and the net obligation.

nodes.title: Note 17 – Postretirement Plans
nodes.summary: Most employees formerly in defined-benefit pension plans have moved to company-funded defined-contribution plans. Major pension plans are trust-funded, with assets reserved for participants and managed for liquidity and long-term obligations. Other postretirement benefits are mainly retiree health care, generally provided until age 65, with lifetime coverage for certain groups, plus limited life insurance. The note explains funded-status measurement and balance-sheet classification, reports 2022–2024 pension and other postretirement benefit income/cost components and presentation in operating or other income, and introduces tables of 2023–2024 changes in benefit obligations, plan assets, and funded status.

nodes.summary: Presents pension and other postretirement benefit amounts recognized on the consolidated statements of financial position at December 31, for 2024 and 2023, including assets, liabilities, and net amounts.
