nodes.title: Assumptions
nodes.summary: The text reports 2024 and 2023 benefit-related dollar figures, then lists weighted-average assumptions used to calculate year-end benefit obligations and subsequent-year periodic costs: discount rates for pension and other postretirement benefits, expected asset returns, compensation increases, and cash-balance interest credits for 2022–2024. It explains the bond-yield-curve method for setting discount rates and the historical and prospective basis for expected returns, including the five-year moving-average asset value and its $7,955 excess over fair value in 2024. It also gives health-care trend rates, ultimate rates, and convergence years for 2022–2024.

nodes.title: Plan Assets
Investment Strategy
nodes.summary: Describes pension investment objectives: fund benefit obligations, maintain liquidity, manage risk, diversify, and earn competitive returns. Strategic allocations are periodically optimized using liability, liquidity, funding, and return considerations, with de-risking as funding improves; benchmarks, monitoring, and rebalancing manage deviations. Reports 2024/2023 actual and target allocations across fixed income, global equity, private equity, real estate/real assets, and hedge funds. Outlines these asset classes’ investments and strategies, managers’ contractual roles, authorized derivative uses, and derivative notionals: fixed income 42.0%/38.3%, and equity and commodities 0.8%/2.1% of pension assets.

nodes.title: Risk Management
nodes.summary: Pension asset risk management covers funded status, interest rate, market, counterparty, liquidity, and operational risks. The approach centers on liability matching and diversification across asset classes, strategies, managers, industries or sectors, and individual holdings. Publicly traded asset guidelines are monitored through the custodian; OTC derivative counterparties are subject to credit limits. Valuation controls include reviews of manager, custodian, and vendor practices, pricing reconciliation, and periodic security-specific testing.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.summary: The text presents pension plan asset fair values at December 31, 2024 and 2023 by asset class and Levels 1–3, plus investments valued at NAV as a practical expedient, cash, receivables and payables. It explains the hierarchy and valuation methods and inputs for fixed income, pooled funds, derivatives, cash, equities, private investments, real estate, real assets and hedge funds, including adjustments for lagged NAVs. It also reconciles Level 3 activity for both years and reports unrealized gains or losses on Level 3 assets still held.

nodes.title: OPB Plan Assets
nodes.summary: OPB assets are mainly held in daily-liquid index funds allocated about 60% to equities and 40% to debt; expected returns do not materially affect benefit costs. Required 2025 pension contributions are expected to be insignificant, with no discretionary contributions planned. Estimated pension and net postretirement benefit payments are listed for 2025–2034. Certain plan termination provisions address benefit funding after an unapproved change in control and U.S. government claims to surplus assets tied to reimbursed contract contributions. Defined contribution plan expenses were $1,670 million in 2024, $1,564 million in 2023, and $1,260 million in 2022. The 2023 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes 12.9 million shares plus available shares from the superseded 2003 plan, allows various equity and cash awards, and is funded mainly with treasury shares, which are considered sufficient for 2025.

nodes.title: Pension Benefits and Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: Describes pension asset return assumptions, expected 2025 contributions, and estimated 2025–2034 pension and postretirement benefit payments. Explains pension-plan termination provisions, including change-in-control benefit funding and potential U.S. government claims on surplus assets. Reports defined contribution plan expenses for 2022–2024. Summarizes the 2023 Incentive Stock Plan’s eligible awards, share authorization, replacement of the 2003 plan, and use of treasury or, if needed, new shares.

Covers pension investment objectives, allocation strategy, asset classes, managers, derivatives, benchmarks, monitoring and rebalancing; risk controls for funding, market, counterparty, liquidity and operations; and 2024–2023 fair values, valuation methods, hierarchy and Level 3 activity. It also describes OPB asset allocation, contributions, benefit-payment estimates, termination and surplus provisions, defined contribution expenses, and the 2023 Incentive Stock Plan’s awards, share authorization and funding.

nodes.title: Pension Cash Flows and Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: The page reports that required pension contributions are not expected to be significant in 2025 and no discretionary contributions are planned. It lists estimated pension and other postretirement benefit payments for 2025–2034. It describes how plan assets would be used following certain unapproved changes in control and terminations, including potential U.S. government claims to assets tied to reimbursed contract contributions. It also notes that eligible employees may participate in defined contribution plans, chiefly 401(k)s, with expenses of $1,670 million in 2024, $1,564 million in 2023, and $1,260 million in 2022.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The 2023 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes 12.9 million shares plus shares available under the prior plan, permits various equity and cash awards, and ended grants under the 2003 plan; awards are funded from treasury shares when available, which the company expects to be sufficient in 2025. Share-based compensation expense and related tax benefits are reported for 2022–2024. Executive stock options generally vest after three years and expire after ten, with certain post-termination exercise rights. 2024 and 2023 grants were immaterial; 2022 included 348,769 premium-priced options with performance-based exercise-price reductions, valued using Monte Carlo assumptions. The text reports 2024 option activity, exercise values and tax benefits for 2022–2024, unrecognized compensation cost, and 2024 vested-option fair value.

nodes.title: Stock Options
nodes.summary: Share-based compensation expense, primarily in total costs and general and administrative expenses with some production costs inventoried, was $409 million, $697 million, and $726 million in 2024, 2023, and 2022; related income tax benefits were $107 million, $157 million, and $178 million. Executive stock options generally vest after three years and expire after ten, with certain post-termination exercise rights; grant fair values use a Monte Carlo model with no dividend yield. 2024–2023 grants were immaterial. In 2022, 348,769 premium-priced options were granted at 120% of market value, potentially reduced to 110% based on performance. The text provides valuation assumptions and 2024 option activity: 903,999 outstanding and 425,705 exercisable at year-end. It also reports exercised-option intrinsic values and tax benefits for 2022–2024, $9 million unrecognized compensation cost expected over 3.1 years, and $32 million fair value for options vested in 2024; none vested in 2022 or 2023.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text describes executive RSU grants in February 2022–2024, an additional March 2024 grant, and an accelerated July 2022 grant, including units and grant-date fair values. It explains three-year vesting, limited retirement-related vesting eligibility, forfeiture upon other termination, and separate labeling of long-term incentive and other RSUs. Values use the average high and low stock prices on grant dates. A 2024 activity table reports beginning, granted, forfeited, distributed, and ending units, undistributed vested units, unrecognized compensation costs, and remaining amortization periods for both RSU categories.

nodes.title: Equity Awards, Compensation Plans, and Shareholders’ Equity
nodes.summary: The page describes 2024 and 2023 executive PRSUs, including grant values, performance-based payouts, safety modifier, vesting, termination treatment, forfeitures, and compensation cost; PBRSUs tied to peer-relative TSR, which paid out at zero in 2023 and had no 2024 outstanding units; the employee stock purchase plan’s 95%-of-market purchase terms, share authorization, and 2024 purchases; deferred compensation plan options, expenses/income, and liabilities; and authorized common and preferred shares at year-end 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Share Balances and Treasury Stock
nodes.summary: A table tracks common, treasury, and mandatory convertible preferred share balances, issuances, and acquisitions from January 1, 2022 through December 31, 2024. On October 30, 2024, 129,375,000 treasury-held common shares with $5.00 par value were issued, generating $18,181 in cash proceeds net of underwriting fees and other issuance costs.

nodes.title: Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock
nodes.summary: On October 31, 2024, the company issued 115 million depositary shares representing 5.75 million 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred shares, with a $1,000 liquidation preference and $1 par value, receiving $5,651 net proceeds. Cumulative dividends may be paid in cash, common shares, or both, quarterly; $72 was declared in December 2024 and paid in cash January 15, 2025. Conversion rates range from 5.8280 to 6.9940 common shares per preferred share based on common-stock market value, subject to adjustments. Unless converted earlier, shares automatically convert October 15, 2027, using a 20-trading-day average price measure. Fundamental changes permit conversion at a specified rate and compensation for accumulated and remaining scheduled dividends; otherwise, holders may elect conversion before that date at 5.8280 shares, subject to adjustments.

nodes.summary: Presents changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) by component for 2022–2024: currency translation adjustments, investment gains and losses, derivative gains and losses, defined-benefit pension and other postretirement benefits, and total balances. Footnotes explain tax treatment, pension remeasurement and amortization reclassifications, cash-flow hedge losses reclassified to other income, and related references to Note 17. nodes.title: Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary:
Cash Flow Hedges
Our cash flow hedges include foreign currency forward contracts, commodity swaps and commodity purchase contracts. We use foreign currency forward contracts to manage currency risk associated with certain expected sales and purchases through 2031. We use commodity derivatives, such as fixed-

nodes.summary:

We have entered into agreements to purchase and sell aluminum to address long-term strategic sourcing objectives and non-U.S. business requirements. nodes.title: Notional Amounts and Fair Values
nodes.summary: The text reports derivative notional amounts and fair values at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including designated and undesignated foreign-exchange and commodity contracts, accrued liabilities, other assets, netting arrangements, and net recorded balances. It summarizes hedge-related gains and losses recognized in OCI and reclassified from AOCI to earnings for 2022–2024 by contract type and income-statement category. In 2022, $50 of cash-flow-hedge losses was moved from AOCI to other income when forecast transactions became unlikely; gains and losses on undesignated derivatives were insignificant. The company expects to reclassify $64 million pre-tax of cash-flow-hedge losses into earnings over the next 12 months. Credit-risk provisions may require settlement or collateral; qualifying contracts had a $22 million net liability at year-end 2024, with no collateral posted.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Impairment
nodes.summary: Defines the three fair value hierarchy levels and presents recurring fair-value assets and derivative liabilities by level for December 31, 2024 and 2023. Describes market-based valuation of money market funds and investments, and income-based valuation of foreign currency and commodity derivatives. Also reports nonrecurring long-lived asset impairment losses and related fair values for 2024 and 2023, covering property, plant and equipment, investments, other assets, and operating lease equipment.

nodes.title: Total
nodes.summary: Note 21 explains the three-level fair value hierarchy and reports recurring fair-value assets and derivative liabilities for 2024 and 2023. It describes market-based valuation of money market funds and investments, and income-based valuation of foreign-currency and commodity derivatives. It summarizes nonrecurring impairment losses and related asset fair values, valuation methods for property, investments, other assets, and operating lease equipment, including aircraft publication values and condition adjustments. It also provides Level 3 aircraft valuation inputs and disclosures of carrying and fair values for notes receivable and debt not otherwise measured at fair value.

nodes.title: Fair Value Valuation Methods and Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: Describes Level 2 and Level 3 valuation methods for property, investments, other assets, and operating lease equipment, including third-party aircraft publications, management review, and asset-specific adjustments. A table reports nonrecurring fair value measurement of operating lease equipment, its market approach, aircraft value publications, condition-adjustment inputs, and related ranges and notes. It also compares carrying amounts with fair values and hierarchy levels for notes receivable and debt at December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: Fair Value of Financial Assets and Liabilities
nodes.summary: Presents December 31, 2023 carrying amounts and fair values for notes receivable and debt, with Level 2 and Level 3 classifications. Notes receivable fair values use discounted cash flows or counterparty financial data; debt values use market yields, dealer quotes, or discounted cash flows. Fair values of indemnifications and financing commitments cannot practicably be estimated. Several other financial instruments are excluded because carrying values approximate fair value at December 31, 2024 and 2023; these use Level 2 inputs, except cash, which is Level 1.

nodes.title: Note 22 – Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: The company faces pending legal proceedings, claims, and government investigations involving products, contracts, employment, securities, and other matters, which may lead to fines, damages, restitution, forfeitures, or restrictions on government contracting, certifications, and exports. It expects no material financial impact from currently pending matters based on available information. Litigation and investigations concern the 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX crashes, including a securities class action and families’ claims. After the Justice Department found Boeing had violated its 2021 deferred prosecution agreement, a proposed guilty plea with a $244 million fine, at least $455 million in safety and compliance investment, and a three-year monitor was rejected by the court in December 2024; discussions continue. The 2024 Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 accident also prompted lawsuits and government inquiries. Boeing cannot estimate potential uninsured losses beyond accrued amounts for these accidents.

nodes.title: Note 23 – Segment and Revenue Information
nodes.summary: The note describes Boeing’s BCA, BDS and BGS segments, their activities and revenue-recognition methods, and how the CEO uses segment operating earnings to allocate resources and monitor results. It reconciles 2022–2024 segment revenues, R&D and other costs to operating results; reports consolidated revenue by customer region, U.S. government share and overseas operating assets; and disaggregates segment revenue by geography, customer, contract type and recognition timing. It also reports equity-method investment income and explains backlog measurement, its $521.3 billion 2024 value, expected conversion timing and risks of reductions or cancellations.

nodes.title: BGS Revenue, Equity Earnings, and Backlog
nodes.summary: The page reports BGS revenues for 2022–2024 by customer type, intersegment eliminations, and revenue-recognition categories, including U.S. government revenue (with foreign military sales). Equity-method income was $104 million in 2024, $70 million in 2023, and $56 million in 2022, driven mainly by BDS investments in 2024–2023 and unallocated items and other in 2022. Backlog was $521.336 billion at year-end 2024; about 14% is expected to convert to revenue by 2025 and 59% by 2028. Conversion timing is uncertain, and delays, production disruptions, or 777X and 737 program entry-into-service delays could reduce backlog or cause cancellations.

nodes.title: Unallocated Items and Benefit Costs
key_items: Pension and Other Postretirement Benefit Expense
nodes.summary: Explains unallocated items, eliminations and other expenses, including shared services, segment cost allocation under U.S. Government Cost Accounting Standards (CAS), and the 2022–2024 expense components. Notes a 2024 $244 million charge tied to a proposed Department of Justice agreement. Describes CAS allocation of pension and postretirement costs, the difference between GAAP and CAS service costs, non-operating benefit expenses, and 2022–2024 FAS/CAS service cost adjustment figures.

nodes.title: Assets, Capital Spending and Depreciation
nodes.summary: Presents segment assets for 2024 and 2023, noting unallocated assets mainly comprise cash, investments, tax assets, capitalized interest, centrally managed assets and eliminations. Reports capital expenditures by segment and year for 2022–2024, with unallocated spending primarily for centrally managed assets. Summarizes depreciation and amortization by segment and centrally managed assets for 2022–2024, explaining that centrally managed costs are allocated by usage and occupancy and giving allocations to BCA, BDS and BGS for each year.

nodes.summary: The independent auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Boeing’s 2024 and 2023 financial position and its results and cash flows for the three years ended 2024 fairly present, in all material respects, under U.S. GAAP. The auditor also reports an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2024. nodes.title: Critical Audit Matters
nodes.summary: Defines critical audit matters as current-period audit issues communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee that concern material financial-statement accounts or disclosures and involve especially challenging, subjective, or complex judgments. nodes.title: Cost Estimates for Fixed-Price Development Contracts — Refer to Notes 1 and 14 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns estimating costs and margins for long-term fixed-price development contracts, where revenue is recognized over time using costs incurred to measure progress. Cost uncertainty, operational and technical complexity, and supply-chain and operational disruptions can reduce margins or cause losses. Estimates for the KC-46A Tanker, Commercial Crew, VC-25B, T-7A, and MQ-25 required extensive auditor effort, judgment, and specialized expertise. Audit work assessed estimation methods, assumptions, outcomes and estimate timing; consulted project personnel; observed work sites; tested data and compared independent estimates; reviewed prior estimates against actual results and related controls; and tested controls over judgments, data, and calculations.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Estimates for the 777X Program — Refer to Notes 1 and 8 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns Boeing’s 777X program accounting estimates. Because no aircraft have been delivered, costs are recorded only if estimated program costs exceed revenue; Boeing recognized about $3.5 billion in reach-forward losses in 2024. Certification uncertainty, production disruptions, schedule delays, and difficulty estimating customer consideration could materially increase losses. Auditing these estimates required substantial effort, specialized expertise, and judgment. Auditors assessed estimation methods and changes, event timelines, certification status, regulatory communications, customer renegotiations and negotiations, and customer communications; searched for contradictory public information; and tested controls over judgments, assumptions, data, extrapolations, and estimates of possible outcomes.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Estimates for the 737 Program — Refer to Notes 1 and 8 to the financial statements
nodes.summary: Deloitte identified Boeing’s 737 program accounting estimates as a critical audit matter because uncertain production schedules—affected by FAA oversight, safety and quality requirements, and supplier constraints—make forecast costs, revenue, and gross margin highly judgmental. Audit work included production-line and management inquiries; review of safety plans, FAA communications, supplier issues, and public reports; schedule and historical-output assessments; delay sensitivity analysis; and testing related controls. Deloitte signed its report February 3, 2025, noting service as auditor since at least 1934. It also opined that Boeing maintained effective internal control over financial reporting at December 31, 2024, describing management and auditor responsibilities, audit standards and procedures, and the purpose and limitations of internal controls.

Management is responsible for controls and its effectiveness assessment. The PCAOB-registered, independent auditors describe their responsibilities and audit procedures, including risk assessment and testing, and state that the audit provides a reasonable basis for their opinion.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Internal control over financial reporting is designed to provide reasonable assurance that external financial statements comply with GAAP. It includes policies and procedures for maintaining accurate records, ensuring authorized transactions are recorded and receipts and expenditures are properly authorized, and preventing or promptly detecting unauthorized asset activity that could materially affect financial statements. Controls may not prevent or detect all misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline due to changing conditions or reduced compliance. The statement is signed by Deloitte & Touche LLP in Chicago on February 3, 2025.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934 (intro)
Description of Capital Stock
nodes.summary: As of December 31, 2024, Boeing had common stock and 6.00% Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock registered under Exchange Act Section 12. The capital-stock summary is governed by the Charter, By-laws, and preferred-stock Certificate of Designations. The Charter authorizes 1.2 billion common and 20 million preferred shares. Common shareholders may receive declared dividends and pro rata distributions subject to preferred rights and agreements; they have one vote per share, no cumulative voting, preemptive, conversion, or redemption rights, and shares are fully paid and non-assessable. Voting thresholds cover ordinary actions, director elections, and specified By-law amendments. The Board may establish preferred-stock series and set their dividends, redemption, liquidation, sinking-fund, voting, preemption, and conversion terms.

nodes.title: Description of Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock
nodes.summary: On October 31, 2024, Boeing issued 115 million NYSE-listed Depositary Shares, each representing one-twentieth of a Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock share. The preferred stock and common shares issued on conversion are fully paid and nonassessable, and holders have no preemptive or preferential purchase rights. The preferred stock itself is not exchange- or quotation-system-listed. Computershare Trust Company, N.A. serves as common stock transfer agent and registrar, and as preferred stock transfer, registrar, conversion, and dividend disbursing agent.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: For dividends and liquidation, winding-up, or dissolution, Boeing’s Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock ranks senior to common stock and other stock not expressly given equal or senior rank; pari passu with stock expressly designated parity; and junior to stock expressly designated senior and to Boeing’s existing and future debt. It is also structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and subsidiary stock held by third parties.

nodes.title: Dividends
nodes.summary: Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock earns cumulative 6% annual dividends on its $1,000 liquidation preference ($60 yearly; $15 per full quarter), payable quarterly through October 15, 2027, if declared and legally funded, in cash, common shares, or both. The text specifies accrual, record and payment dates, business-day adjustments, and full- and partial-period calculations; unpaid dividends earn no interest, and all prior dividends must be provided for before further dividends. It describes legal and debt-related limits, restrictions on junior-stock distributions and repurchases and their exceptions, proportional treatment of parity-stock dividends, and confirms preferred holders do not share in other distributions. Convertible debt securities remain outside the restrictions; withholding taxes may be deducted from cash or share payments.

nodes.title: Method of Payment of Dividends
nodes.summary: Boeing may pay declared dividends on mandatory convertible preferred stock in cash, common shares, or a combination, and must notify holders of any share election and the split between payment methods by the earlier of the declaration date or the tenth scheduled trading day before payment. Shares are valued at 97% of the five-day average VWAP; fractional shares receive cash adjustments. If reasonably required, Boeing will use commercially reasonable efforts to register and maintain resale availability, qualify shares under state laws, and secure exchange listing. Share payments are capped using a $50.04 floor price, adjusted for anti-dilution; any elected dividend amount exceeding the value of shares delivered must be paid in cash if legally possible.

nodes.title: No Redemption
nodes.summary:
No Redemption
Boeing may not redeem the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock. However, at Boeing’s option, Boeing may purchase the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock or Depositary Shares from time to time in the open market, by tender offer, exchange offer or otherwise.

nodes.title: Liquidation Preference
nodes.summary: In Boeing’s liquidation, winding-up or dissolution, Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock holders are entitled to $1,000 per share plus accrued, unpaid dividends, after creditor and senior-stock claims but before junior stock. If preferred and parity-stock claims cannot be paid in full, they share assets equally and ratably according to their entitlements; preferred holders have no claim to remaining assets after full payment. An asset or business sale, merger or consolidation is not itself a liquidation. The Certificate of Designations does not require funds to be reserved for the preference, despite its amount substantially exceeding par value.

nodes.title: Voting Rights
nodes.summary: Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock generally has no voting rights except those required by law or specified. After dividends go unpaid for six or more periods, holders vote with other voting preferred stock to elect up to two additional directors, subject to independence limits; a 25% holder request can trigger an election, and voting is weighted by liquidation preference. Rights end when arrears are cured, terminating those directors’ terms and reducing the Board by two; removal and vacancy-filling rules apply. While shares remain outstanding, two-thirds holder approval is required for senior stock, materially adverse amendments, or certain mergers and reclassifications, subject to stated exceptions and protections for equivalent successor securities. Boeing may make non-adverse or corrective amendments without consent.

nodes.title: Mandatory Conversion
nodes.summary: Outstanding preferred shares automatically convert on the mandatory conversion date. If dividends through October 15, 2027 are undeclared by October 1, the conversion rate is increased for unpaid dividends using the greater of the floor price or 97% of the five-day average price; any specified excess is paid pro rata in cash if legally permitted. Excluding dividend-related shares, conversion is 5.8280 shares above the $171.5854 threshold price; between that threshold and the $142.9797 initial price, $1,000 divided by market value (5.8280–6.9940 shares); and 6.9940 shares below the initial price. The threshold represents about 20% appreciation over the initial price. Fixed rates and market value are subject to anti-dilution adjustments.

Describes Boeing’s common and 6.00% Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock registered under Exchange Act Section 12, including authorized shares, common-stock rights and voting thresholds, and the Board’s authority to establish preferred-stock terms. Covers the preferred offering and depositary shares, agents, ranking and subordination, cumulative dividends and payment methods, restrictions, redemption, liquidation preference, voting and protective rights, and automatic conversion rates, dividend adjustments, and anti-dilution provisions.

nodes.title: Definitions
Definitions (intro)
nodes.summary: Defines applicable market value as average VWAP during a 20-trading-day final averaging period before October 15, 2027, and the expected mandatory conversion date as October 15, 2027. It specifies trading and scheduled trading days, market disruption events, VWAP sources and fallback calculation, and averaging. Holders may optionally convert at least one preferred share before October 15, 2027, outside a fundamental change conversion period, into common stock at the minimum rate, subject to adjustments. Undeclared unpaid dividends may generate additional shares based on the greater of the floor price or early conversion average price, with no cash payment for any shortfall. Otherwise, unpaid dividends are not paid upon conversion, except declared dividends payable after the relevant record date to the holder of record.

nodes.title: General
nodes.summary: If a defined fundamental change occurs by October 15, 2027, preferred shareholders may convert during a limited period at a specified conversion rate and receive a dividend make-whole: the discounted value of future dividends plus any accumulated unpaid dividends, with Boeing allowed to pay some or all in common shares. A declared dividend payable after the relevant record date remains payable to record-date holders and is excluded from the make-whole. The conversion window begins on the effective date and ends 20 days after it or notice, whichever is later, but never after October 15, 2027; Boeing must notify holders within two business days. Nonconverting holders receive neither the special rate nor make-whole. Fundamental changes include specified control acquisitions, stock or asset transactions, and delisting, subject to an exception for qualifying transactions in which at least 90% of consideration is listed common stock and the preferred stock converts into that consideration. If another entity’s securities replace Boeing common stock, references to Boeing in the definition shift to that entity.

nodes.title: Fundamental change conversion rate
nodes.summary: The fundamental change conversion rate is determined by the transaction’s effective date and stock price: cash consideration uses cash paid per share; otherwise, stock price is the average Common Stock VWAP over the five trading days ending immediately before the change. Table stock-price headings are adjusted when minimum conversion rates change, and table rates are adjusted alongside fixed conversion rates under the anti-dilution provisions. The table lists rates for specified prices and dates. Unlisted values use straight-line interpolation by price and date, using a 365- or 366-day year; prices above $210 (as adjusted) yield the minimum rate, and prices below $100 (as adjusted) yield the maximum rate.

nodes.title: Make-whole dividend amount
nodes.summary: For preferred shares converted during a fundamental-change period, Boeing may pay the make-whole dividend in cash, common shares, or both; cash is the default unless Boeing elects shares by the second business day after the change. Shares are valued at 97% of the stock price, with fractional shares settled in cash using the specified five-day average VWAP. Share payments are capped using the greater of the floor price or 97% of the stock price, with qualifying excess paid in cash if legally permitted. If Delaware law prevents payment or delivery, the conversion rate increases for the unpaid amount, but Boeing need not pay any resulting shortfall. Boeing must notify holders within two business days of the conversion rate, make-whole amount and payment method, and accumulated dividends and payment method. The payment and delivery obligations may be challenged as penalties under reasonableness principles. The text then introduces conversion procedures.

nodes.title: Upon mandatory conversion
nodes.summary: On the mandatory conversion date, all outstanding Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock automatically converts into Common Stock. Recipients become record holders at 5:00 p.m. New York City time that day. Before then, except as provided under anti-dilution adjustments, the conversion shares are not considered outstanding, and preferred-stock holders have no associated Common Stock rights, including voting, tender-offer response, or dividend and distribution rights.

nodes.title: Upon early conversion
nodes.summary: For early conversion before October 15, 2027, holders must follow the applicable conversion procedures: beneficial owners of global shares submit DTC’s required instruction form, while certificated holders follow the Certificate of Designations. The conversion date is when requirements are satisfied, but cannot be after October 15, 2027. Holders generally owe no issuance or delivery taxes or duties, except those arising from transfers into another name; stock and any cash are delivered no earlier than the second business day after conversion and only after applicable taxes and duties are paid. Recipients become record holders at 5:00 p.m. New York City time on the conversion date; before then, the shares are not outstanding and confer no associated rights, including voting, tender-offer, dividend, or distribution rights.

nodes.title: Fractional shares
Fractional shares (intro)
nodes.summary: No fractional common shares are issued when Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock is converted. The holder instead receives cash, rounded to the nearest cent, equal to the fractional share amount multiplied by the average Common Stock VWAP over the five trading days ending on the second trading day before conversion. When multiple preferred shares are surrendered by or for one holder at once, the conversion share count is calculated using their aggregate.

nodes.title: Anti-dilution Adjustments
nodes.summary: The text sets out anti-dilution adjustments to Boeing preferred stock conversion rates for common-stock dividends, discounted rights or warrants, stock splits, asset and spin-off distributions, cash dividends, and qualifying tender or exchange offers. It specifies formulas, valuation periods, effective dates, reversals for distributions not completed, special holder entitlements for large distributions and rights plans, and the definition of ex-date and current market price. It also covers discretionary adjustments, potential tax and withholding consequences, calculation thresholds and rounding, participation-based exceptions, transactions excluded from adjustment, notice and rate disclosures, corresponding floor-price changes, VWAP-period adjustments, and post-averaging-period dividend treatment.

nodes.title: Recapitalizations, Reclassifications and Changes in Common Stock
nodes.summary: The text defines reorganization events, including specified mergers, asset transfers, stock reclassifications, and statutory or binding exchanges that convert Common Stock into other consideration. Outstanding Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock then converts, without holder consent, into the exchange property its holder would have received by converting to Common Stock before the event. For mixed consideration, exchange property is the weighted average actually received, which Boeing must report. Conversion and dividend calculations use exchange-property units, subject to exclusions for prior-record-date distributions. The Board determines unit values in good faith, using specified market-price or independent-bank valuation methods for listed shares or ADRs. Boeing or a successor must notify holders in writing within 20 calendar days of the event and exchange property; failure to notify does not affect these provisions.

nodes.title: Reservation of Shares
nodes.summary: Boeing must reserve sufficient authorized, unissued or treasury common shares, free of preemptive rights, to cover conversion of all outstanding Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, including the maximum additional conversion amount. Depositary Shares are issued under an agreement with Computershare and each represents 1/20 of a preferred share, initially evidenced by a global security, with proportional rights and voting powers. “Holders” means registered owners, not indirect DTC beneficial owners. Conversion elections must be in lots of 20 Depositary Shares, at an adjustable minimum rate of 0.2914 common shares per share on an early conversion date or at the fundamental-change rate during the applicable period; the text refers to a table setting that rate by change date and stock price and to related preferred-stock terms.

nodes.title: Depositary Shares and General Terms
nodes.summary: Boeing deposited the preferred stock underlying the Depositary Shares under an agreement with Computershare Trust Company, N.A., Computershare Inc. as joint bank depositary, and holders. Each Depositary Share represents one-twentieth of a Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock share, initially evidenced by a global security, and carries proportional rights, preferences, privileges, and voting powers under the agreement. “Holders” means registered owners, not beneficial owners holding through DTC. The preceding text also describes reserving sufficient Common Stock for conversion, including the maximum additional conversion amount, free of preemptive or similar rights.

nodes.title: Conversion
nodes.summary: Depositary Shares, each representing 1/20 of a preferred share, convert only in lots of 20, either early at an adjustable minimum rate or during a fundamental-change period at a rate determined by stock price and effective date. A table provides rates across dates and prices; interpolation applies between entries, with maximum/minimum rates outside the table’s price range. Converted holders receive their proportional common stock and cash; applicable taxes may be withheld. General conversion rates depend on common-stock market value. Shares are delivered through DTC or certificates; fractional shares are paid in cash using a specified five-day VWAP, aggregating multiple shares surrendered. Dividends equal 1/20 of preferred dividends, flow through DTC or the depositary, and have specified expected amounts and matching record dates; fractional dividend shares receive cash adjustments, and taxes or charges may reduce or block distributions and transfers. Boeing cannot redeem Depositary Shares but may purchase them through market or offer transactions.

nodes.title: Depositary Share Dividends, Distributions and Redemption
nodes.summary: Depositary Share dividends equal one-twentieth of the related preferred-stock dividend, with DTC payment procedures, proportional distribution by the depositary, expected dividend amounts, and matching record dates. Fractional common shares distributed as dividends or issued on conversion are paid in cash using the specified five-day VWAP; multiple conversions are aggregated. Distributions may be reduced or withheld for taxes, including withholding from cash or shares. Boeing cannot redeem Depositary Shares but may purchase them through market or offer transactions.

nodes.title: Voting the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock
nodes.summary: Each Depositary Share represents a 1/20 interest in Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock and carries 1/20 of a vote when preferred holders may vote. The depositary will notify receipt holders of voting meetings; holders on the matching record date may instruct how their represented shares should be voted. The depositary will endeavor to follow instructions, with Boeing providing necessary assistance, and will abstain where it receives no specific instructions.

nodes.title: Modification, Amendment and Termination
nodes.summary: Boeing may amend the deposit agreement without holder consent for specified corrective or administrative purposes, provided changes generally do not materially harm holders’ rights. Other amendments require approval by holders of a majority of outstanding Depositary Shares, and certain fundamental changes require consent from each affected holder, including changes to consent thresholds, payments, withdrawals, currency, enforcement, conversion, or voting rights. The agreement may be terminated only after all shares are cancelled or final liquidation distributions are made. Boeing pays specified taxes and initial-deposit fees; holders pay other specified charges, including withdrawal fees. Each 20 Depositary Shares may be exchanged for one preferred share and associated property, subject to transfer taxes in certain cases; preferred shares cannot be redeposited for Depositary Shares.

nodes.title: Depositary Share Rights, Fees, and Withdrawals
nodes.summary: The text lists deposit-agreement changes requiring protection of holders’ consent, payment, surrender, currency, enforcement, conversion, and voting rights, and permits termination only after all shares are cancelled or final liquidation distributions are completed. Boeing pays specified taxes, governmental charges, and initial deposit fees; holders pay other specified charges, including withdrawal fees. Holders may exchange 20 Depositary Shares for one preferred share and associated property, subject to transfer taxes in certain cases, but cannot deposit preferred shares to obtain Depositary Shares.

nodes.title: Depositary Shares: Listing, Form and Notices
nodes.summary: The Depositary Shares are listed on the NYSE as BA-PRA, and Boeing will use reasonable best efforts to maintain the listing. Listing does not ensure a market, market depth, or easy resale; no separate public market is expected for the preferred stock apart from the Depositary Shares. The preferred stock will be registered to the bank depositary, while Depositary Shares will be issued in DTC book-entry form before conversion. The depositary will forward required Boeing reports, notices, and communications to Depositary Share holders. A Book-entry, Settlement and Clearance section is also identified.

Boeing cannot redeem Depositary Shares but may purchase them.

nodes.title: The global security
nodes.summary: Depositary Shares were initially issued as one registered global security, held by the bank depositary as DTC’s custodian and registered to DTC’s nominee, Cede & Co. Beneficial ownership is limited to DTC participants and persons holding through them, with ownership and transfers recorded in DTC’s and participants’ records. nodes.title: Book-entry procedures for the global security
nodes.summary: The text explains that global-security interests are governed by DTC’s book-entry procedures, based on information Boeing considers reliable but does not guarantee and which may change. It describes DTC’s legal status, custody and servicing role, electronic settlement functions, direct and indirect participants, and SEC-filed rules. Dividends and other payments flow through DTC to participants, with Boeing and the depositary disclaiming responsibility for beneficial-interest records and payments; participant practices govern onward payments. It then presents Boeing’s Global Annual Incentive Plan, effective January 1, 2025, consolidating three prior plans to attract and retain employees, reward business-supporting performance, and link contributions to company results. nodes.title: Introduction
Introduction (intro)
nodes.summary: The text outlines Boeing’s Executive Supplemental Savings Plan’s four components, history and 2025 amendments, and its 409A/ERISA status. It defines accounts, administrators, eligible employers and employees, compensation, deferrals, contributions, beneficiaries, service, separation, and related terms. It then explains annual and midyear eligibility and deferral limits, election and distribution choices, evergreen elections, deadlines, irrevocability and cancellations—including post-separation restrictions and emergency exceptions—and when deferrals are credited. It introduces Article IV on company contributions.

nodes.title: 4.1 Restoration Matching Contributions
nodes.summary: Participants making Base Pay deferrals under a timely Restoration Deferral Election receive a Company Restoration Matching Contribution, calculated using the applicable Boeing 401(k) Plan Year matching formula. The match applies only to Restoration Deferrals, not Extra Deferrals, and is credited to the Account when the related deferrals are credited. Distribution elections are addressed in Article VI.

nodes.title: 4.2 Restoration True-Up Contributions
nodes.summary: The Company may make discretionary Restoration True-Up Contributions for eligible employees, generally equal to the Boeing 401(k) true-up match calculated for the Plan Year (or the period before contributions stopped due to tax-code limits), less any actual 401(k) true-up match. No contribution is made if employment ends before the Plan Year’s last business day, except for specified retirement, Social Security Administration-determined disability, layoff, or death. Combined matching and restoration contributions may not exceed 100% of the first 10% of eligible compensation, and Boeing 401(k) true-up eligibility requirements apply. A timely Restoration Deferral Election is not required. Contributions are credited when 401(k) true-ups are made, or as soon as administratively feasible; distribution elections are addressed in Article VI.

nodes.title: 4.3 Incentive Matching Contributions
nodes.summary: Participants making Cash Incentive Deferrals may receive Company Incentive Matching Contributions calculated using the percentage in their Boeing 401(k) matching formula for the Plan Year. Eligibility requires a timely deferral election; distribution elections are addressed in Article VI. Matching contributions are credited when the related deferrals are credited. No match applies to incentives paid, or otherwise payable, after Separation from Service, except when separation results from commencing Pilot Early Leave.

nodes.title: 4.4 Company Non-Elective Contributions (Component of the Executive Benefit)
nodes.summary: The Company may make non-elective contributions for selected eligible employees under Compensation Committee or delegate-set terms. For 2022 and 2023, the contribution includes 2% of eligible Base Pay and Cash Incentive, subject to employment through the final business day of the year, except for specified retirement, disability, layoff, or death; post-termination incentive pay is excluded. For employees promoted to the US Executive Payroll, qualifying pre-promotion pay may be included under Administrator rules. Deferrals are not required for eligibility. Contributions are credited when made to the Boeing 401(k), or on another designated date, as soon as administratively feasible; distribution elections are addressed in Article VI.

nodes.title: 4.5 DC SERP Contributions (Component of the Executive Benefit)
(i) Hired Between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019
nodes.summary: The text establishes eligibility for DC SERP Contributions by Plan Year, subject to exclusions: no contributions for elected officers on or after January 1, 2020; employees hired or promoted onto the US Executive Payroll on or after that date; or former elected officers, unless the Chief Human Resources Officer, after consulting the Compensation Committee, determines cessation was unrelated to planned termination. Employees hired from January 1, 2009 through December 31, 2019 qualify under subsection (i) if they are in level EL or EV (formerly E-1 to E-3) and were on the Executive Payroll at any E-1–E-5 level on December 31, 2019, are not elected officers, and cannot accrue benefits under a Controlled Group defined benefit plan.

nodes.title: (ii) Hired Before January 1, 2009
nodes.summary: Employees hired before January 1, 2009 qualify under this category if they were on the US Executive Payroll at level E-1 through E-5 on December 31, 2019, and are not elected Company officers. “Hired” usually means the latest Company hire or rehire date, subject to rules: direct returns from approved leave (including qualifying ULA or USA service) and uninterrupted Controlled Group transfers are not rehires; layoffs generally do not count as rehires if return occurs within six years, except when the employee started retirement benefits during that period. Certain group-acquired employees joining after September 30, 2008, and before January 1, 2009, are treated as hired on or after January 1, 2009, and receive no contributions before that date. Eligible employees participate while they meet the Section 4.5(A) conditions; eligible participants receive contributions as described in the Plan.

nodes.title: (i) Payroll Contributions
nodes.summary: Payroll contributions are credited when Base Pay and Cash Incentive would be payable, or as soon as administratively feasible. For participants hired January 1, 2009–December 31, 2019, each applicable pay period’s contribution is 2% at level EV (formerly E-2/E-3) or 4% at level EL (formerly E-1), based on level at period-end if it changes during the period. For participants hired before January 1, 2009, the credit is 5%, plus, if age 55 by a Plan Year’s end, 0.5% per whole year of Benefit Service determined January 1, 2016. This supplement is limited to seven aggregate lifetime years, beginning on the latest applicable date: January 1, 2016, January 1 of the year age 55 is reached, or promotion to the US Executive Payroll. For both groups, eligible Base Pay and Cash Incentive must relate to US Executive Payroll service during the pay period; post-termination incentive pay counts only if paid by the final regular paycheck.

nodes.title: (ii) One-Time Contribution
nodes.summary: Eligible employees first promoted during the Plan Year to EL/EV (or, before August 15, 2022, E-1 through E-3) receive a one-time contribution equal to 2% of post-promotion base pay plus the cash-incentive target amount, multiplied by whole years of service since their most recent hire. It is credited at promotion or as soon as feasible; recipients cannot receive another under this provision. Article V outlines vesting and forfeitures: Extra Deferral, Restoration, and, subject to exceptions, Executive Benefit Accounts are fully vested. The Administrator may forfeit post-2016 legacy Executive SSP+ contributions for specified misconduct, including qualifying felony convictions during employment or within five years after termination.

The section defines DC SERP eligibility and contribution rules for executive employees hired before 2009 or from 2009–2019, including payroll-level, officer, and defined-benefit-plan exclusions and rules for determining hire or rehire dates. It describes recurring payroll credits by hire group, level, age, and service, plus a one-time promotion contribution based on pay and years of service. It also addresses participation, credit timing, vesting, forfeitures, and misconduct-related forfeiture of certain legacy contributions.

nodes.title: Vesting and Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: Article V sets out vesting and forfeiture rules for certain Plan benefits and refers readers to provisions on missing participants and improper credits, anti-assignment, the Plan’s unfunded status, and DCP Account forfeitures. Extra Deferral and Restoration Accounts are always 100% vested; Executive Benefit Accounts are also 100% vested at all times, subject to Sections 5.5 and 5.6.

nodes.title: 5.5 Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: The Administrator may forfeit some or all legacy Executive SSP+ Company Contributions made from January 1, 2017, for misconduct during employment or within five years after termination: certain felony offenses against the Controlled Group or its interests; competition or adverse business activity, including inducing workers or contractors to leave without required senior HR approval; disparaging statements; or misuse or disclosure of confidential information. Exceptions protect legally protected government communications and sworn testimony. The Administrator may seek legal or equitable recovery of amounts already paid. A court may narrow unenforceable terms to the broadest enforceable scope. In appropriate cases, contributions tied to cash incentives subject to a plan clawback must also be reimbursed.

nodes.title: 5.6 DC SERP Vesting
nodes.summary: DC SERP payments are limited to vested account amounts. Participants hired in 2009–2019 generally vest fully after 36 consecutive months at eligible executive level, death while employed, or qualifying layoff; those hired before 2009 vest fully after 36 consecutive months on the US Executive Payroll, qualifying death, or layoff. For 2009–2019 hires meeting age 55/10 years’ service or 62/1, payroll contributions vest after 36 months, while one-time contributions vest monthly at 1/36, subject to death or layoff acceleration. Authorized absences count toward service, but other breaks cannot be combined. Certain uninterrupted comparable executive service with ULA or USA counts under transfer conditions. Separation or transfer may forfeit unvested payroll contributions; resumed service does not vest later one-time accruals until applicable requirements are met. Components vest separately, with rules for rehire and already-vested components. Forfeitures are not reinstated; related provisions address missing participants, improper credits, anti-assignment, and the plan’s unfunded status.

nodes.title: 5.7 DC SERP Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: The Administrator may forfeit some or all of a participant’s DC SERP Account for specified conduct during employment or within five years after termination: felony theft, fraud, embezzlement, or similar harmful unlawful acts; competition with Controlled Group business or unauthorized solicitation of its employees, representatives, or consultants; disparaging statements; and, for contributions made from January 1, 2017, misuse or disclosure of confidential information. Exceptions protect legally protected government communications and sworn testimony. The Administrator may seek legal or equitable recovery of benefits already paid. A court may narrow unenforceable provisions to their broadest enforceable scope. Appropriate amounts tied to incentive awards subject to a Cash Incentive plan’s clawback must also be forfeited or reimbursed.

nodes.title: 6.1 Form and Timing of Distribution
nodes.summary: Participants may elect distribution timing and form for Extra Deferral and Restoration Accounts; absent timely elections, payment defaults to a lump sum in January after separation, with a legacy Boeing election applying to certain Extra Deferrals. Executive Benefit Accounts default to the same lump-sum timing. Benefits may be paid as a lump sum or 2–15 annual installments, with account valuation rules and no post-valuation earnings; installment balances of $10,000 or less are cashed out. Elections may generally be changed once per subaccount, subject to advance notice, a 12-month delay, at least five years’ additional deferral, age/separation limits, and no changes after installments begin. Payments must start by the January following separation and attainment of age 70½. Specified Employees face a six-month payment delay, subject to timing rules and a death exception. Unforeseeable emergencies permit limited distributions from specified accounts, but not the DC SERP portion.

nodes.title: 6.2 Death Benefits
nodes.summary: If a Participant dies before their Account is fully distributed, the remaining balance is paid to their Beneficiary according to the Participant’s filed or deemed election, in the same form and at the same time as payments would have been made to the Participant (or as soon as administratively feasible after the Company is notified). If the Beneficiary later dies before receiving all amounts, unpaid amounts go to the Beneficiary’s designated beneficiary or beneficiaries; if none are designated or they do not survive, the amounts are paid to the Beneficiary’s estate in a lump sum as soon as administratively feasible.

nodes.title: 6.3 Rehires and Authorized Periods of Absence/Reduced Level of Services
nodes.summary: Section 6.3 explains payment rules for rehired participants and those on authorized absence or reduced services, distinguishing whether benefits have begun. Forfeited nonvested DC SERP accounts are not restored on rehire. After benefits begin, old-account installments continue; new-account payments follow the prior election and generally await separation after rehire. Contributions during qualifying absences or reduced service are paid under the prior election, generally in the next January. Before benefits begin, vested old accounts and new or absence-period accounts follow the prior timing and payment-form election, subject to change rules; age and separation requirements apply as specified, even if service resumes.

nodes.title: Participant Accounts and 2019 Transfers
nodes.summary: The Administrator maintains an account for each participant for each employment period, beginning when the participant becomes Plan-eligible and ending at separation from service. Accounts receive deferrals, company contributions, and earnings credits, and are reduced by payments. In the 2019 restatement, specified participants’ Restoration Benefit sub-account balances were transferred to the SSP, with opening balances matching their Plan balances at December 31, 2018; eligibility categories are defined by SSP employment status and prior participation, including certain individuals never on the Plan’s US Executive Payroll.

nodes.title: 7.2 Earnings Credits
nodes.summary: Participants or beneficiaries may elect earnings credits under the Interest Fund, Boeing Stock Fund, or eligible Other Investment Funds methods, subject to administrator rules; absent an election, the Interest Fund applies. Interest subaccounts adjust daily, using an annual rate based on the mean high and low AA industrial bond yields during the first 11 months of the preceding year, rounded to the nearest quarter-percent, with annual notice. Boeing stock units mirror the Boeing 401(k) fund’s valuation and adjustments but confer no ownership, and reflect stock-related adjustments. Other funds mirror eligible Boeing 401(k) investment funds, excluding Boeing Stock and Stable Value, though the Administrator may disregard elections. Account earnings may receive procedural valuation adjustments, but amounts already distributed are excluded.

nodes.title: 7.3 Investment Election Changes and Restrictions
nodes.summary: Participants may change investment directions for future account additions anytime during the Plan Year, subject to Administrator rules, and transfer subaccounts between funds daily, but cannot transfer between the same funds and back on the same day. After transferring out of the Boeing Stock Fund, they cannot transfer into it for 30 calendar days, regardless of transfer size. They may still direct future additions to that fund and transfer out at any time, subject to insider trading rules.

nodes.title: 7.4 Missing Participants and Improper Credits
nodes.summary: A participant’s account may be forfeited or reduced, even if fully vested, if the Administrator cannot locate the participant or beneficiary to distribute funds, or if the Administrator recaptures improperly credited amounts. Related provisions address anti-assignment and the Plan’s unfunded nature.

nodes.title: 8.1 Plan Administration
nodes.summary: The Administrator oversees the Plan and may establish rules, interpret its terms, determine facts, perform calculations, and require electronic or telephone systems for participant elections and designations. Its decisions—including eligibility and benefit calculations—are conclusive and binding on all persons. The Administrator must periodically report on Plan operations to the Compensation Committee.

nodes.title: 8.2 Claims Procedure
nodes.summary: Claims for Plan benefits and appeals of denials follow the Boeing 401(k) procedures. For elected officers, the Board’s Compensation Committee replaces the Administrator in reviewing claims and appeals, except decisions on potential forfeiture or reimbursement under Sections 5.5 and 5.7, which remain with the Administrator. Section 10.8 addresses limits on subsequent legal action.

Introduces Boeing’s Executive Supplemental Savings Plan, its history, components, legal status, key definitions, eligibility, deferral elections and limits, deadlines, cancellations, and crediting. Covers company matching, true-up, non-elective, and DC SERP contributions; vesting, forfeitures, and misconduct-related recovery; distribution forms, timing, death benefits, rehires, absences, and emergencies; participant accounts, 2019 transfers, earnings credits, investment elections, missing participants and improper credits; and plan administration and claims and appeals procedures.

nodes.title: Amendment and Termination
Amendment and Termination (intro)
nodes.summary: The Plan may be amended by the Board, Compensation Committee, Administrator, or their delegates, but only the Compensation Committee may change Company-provided benefit rates or amounts for U.S. Executive Payroll employees; the Board may terminate the Plan. Following amendment or termination, benefits cannot fall below the amount due upon termination of employment just before the change, adjusted for subsequent Earnings Credits. Distributions generally follow Article VI, though Boeing may pay lump sums upon full Plan termination when permitted by Code section 409A. The Plan creates no employment rights; benefits cannot be assigned or subjected to legal process, and accounts may be reduced for unreimbursed taxes paid on a participant’s behalf. The Plan is unfunded: any supporting trusts remain subject to general creditors, and participants have only unsecured creditor claims. Payments may be delayed or accelerated as permitted by section 409A. The text also begins a provision concerning current income taxation of accounts under section 409A.

nodes.title: Plan Employment, Benefit, and Funding Rules
nodes.summary: The Plan grants no employment rights and does not limit the employer’s ability to terminate employment. Benefits cannot be assigned, transferred, pledged, or reached through legal process; prohibited attempts are void and may lead the Administrator to forfeit benefits. Accounts may also be reduced for unreimbursed taxes paid on an individual’s behalf. The Plan is unfunded: any supporting trust assets remain subject to general creditors, and participants have only unsecured creditor claims. Benefit payments may be delayed or accelerated as permitted by Code section 409A.

nodes.title: 10.5 Involuntary Inclusion in Income
nodes.summary: If an account is determined to be currently taxable under Code section 409A, its taxable portion is immediately distributed; the Plan is intended to comply with section 409A and must be construed accordingly. Federal law governs validity, with Illinois law applying where permitted; invalid provisions do not affect the remainder. Benefit lawsuits must be filed within 180 days after an appeal decision or the deadline for one; Illinois law and courts in Cook County govern, subject to federal preemption. The Company or Controlled Group may withhold required taxes, including specified FICA taxes and related withholding from payments or accounts. Participants remain responsible for tax liabilities exceeding amounts withheld.

nodes.title: Plan Compliance, Legal Rules, and Tax Withholding
nodes.summary: The page states that deferred amounts are intended to comply with Code Section 409A. The Plan is construed under federal law and, where permitted, Illinois law; invalid provisions do not affect the rest. Benefit lawsuits must be filed within 180 days after an appeal decision or the appeal-decision deadline, and participants consent to courts in Cook County, Illinois, subject to federal preemption. The Company may withhold required taxes, including specified FICA taxes and related withholding from payments or accounts; participants remain responsible for excess individual tax liabilities.

nodes.title: Benefit Liability, Overpayments, and Notices
nodes.summary: Benefit payments are solely the responsibility of the employer that employed the participant when contributions were made, unless another entity expressly assumed liability; payments by others do not create shared liability. The Plan may recover overpayments by offsetting future benefits or, if impractical, taking reasonable recovery actions. Required or permitted notices must be written and hand-delivered or sent by registered or certified mail to the specified company or individual address, and are effective upon delivery or the mailing receipt’s postmark date.

The Plan may be amended by authorized parties, with changes to specified U.S. executive benefit rates reserved to the Compensation Committee; the Board may terminate it. Benefits are protected at the pre-change termination amount, adjusted for later earnings credits, and distributions generally follow Article VI, subject to permitted lump sums and timing changes under Code Section 409A. The Plan creates no employment rights; benefits cannot be assigned or reached by legal process, accounts may be reduced for taxes, and the unfunded Plan gives participants only unsecured claims. Taxable accounts may be distributed immediately. Federal and, where permitted, Illinois law govern; benefit suits have a 180-day deadline and Cook County venue. The Company may withhold taxes, while participants remain responsible for excess liabilities. The employing entity is responsible for benefits absent an express assumption; overpayments may be recovered, and notices must be written and delivered or mailed as specified.
